articles.title: Washington Post fired Karen Attiah over social-media posts in 2025; an arbitrator has now ordered her reinstated with full back pay
articles.summary: US News: Karen Attiah, a former Washington Post opinion writer and the newspaper's founding global opinions editor, was fired on September 11, 2025, one day af.
articles.body: Karen Attiah, a former Washington Post opinion writer and the newspaper's founding global opinions editor, was fired on September 11, 2025, one day after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot and killed during a public appearance at Utah Valley University. The Post's termination letter accused Attiah of gross misconduct, saying her social-media comments about Kirk's death violated the newspaper's social-media policies, harmed the organisation's integrity and potentially endangered staff. Nearly a year later, independent arbitrator Sarah Miller Espinosa ruled that the Post did not have âgood and sufficient causeâ to terminate Attiah and had violated its collective bargaining agreement with the Washington-Baltimore News Guild. Espinosa ordered the newspaper to reinstate Attiah immediately, with full back pay and lost benefits. The decision is dated August 20, 2026, but was made public four days later, on August 24. The ruling brought a year-long dispute over newsroom discipline and expression to a close.What Karen Attiah posted after Charlie Kirk's killingAttiah made several posts on Bluesky following Kirk's death, discussing political violence and the public reaction to his killing. In one, she wrote that refusing to engage in what she called âperformative mourningâ for âa white man that espoused violenceâ was not itself violence. In another, she criticised what she described as the expectation that people show âcare, empty goodness and absolutionâ toward white men who espouse hatred and violence. Those posts were cited by the Post in the termination letter that ended her employment the following day. At the time, Attiah had spent 11 years at the newspaper, working as both an editor and opinion writer. She focused particularly on race, gender and international human rights and was the last Black full-time member of the Post's opinion desk when she was fired.Why the arbitrator found the Post did not have sufficient cause to fire herThe arbitration hearing took place June 4, 2026. In her ruling, Espinosa found that the Post had failed to establish that Attiah engaged in gross misconduct and had not shown âgood and sufficient causeâ to terminate her employment. The decision concluded that the firing violated the collective bargaining agreement between the newspaper and the Washington-Baltimore News Guild. Espinosa also rejected the Post's interpretation of Attiah's posts as racial or gender-based disparagement. The ruling said it was not reasonable to conclude that the posts referred to or disparaged all white men, or a particular white man, on the basis of race or gender. It also stated that recognising a person's race or gender does not by itself constitute disparagement on those grounds.The ruling noted that Attiah had worked at the Post for 11 years and had not previously been disciplined. Espinosa concluded that the newspaper had not met the standard required under the union agreement to justify termination without progressive discipline. She described the termination penalty as âabsolutely disproportionalâ and ordered the newspaper to reinstate Attiah immediately, with full back pay and lost benefits.What Attiah said after winning the arbitration caseAttiah publicly announced the ruling after the decision became public, saying that an independent arbitrator had ordered the Post to reinstate her with back pay. In a statement, she said the decision confirmed that she had been doing her job as an opinion writer and that doing that job was not misconduct. She added that she was ârelieved to finally have that record set straight.â The Washington-Baltimore News Guild and the Democracy Defenders Fund, which supported her case, welcomed the ruling as a significant victory for the union and press freedom. The Washington Post said it respects the arbitration process and declined to comment further on the ruling.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Cash buyers dominated the US housing boom. Now financed buyers are fighting back
articles.summary: News News: Cash is losing some of its advantage in the US housing market as home sales slow, inventory increases and price growth moderates, giving buyers relyin.
articles.body: Cash is losing some of its advantage in the US housing market as home sales slow, inventory increases and price growth moderates, giving buyers relying on mortgages a better chance of competing.The share of homes bought with cash fell to 31.4% in the first four months of 2026, from 32.3% during the same period a year earlier, according to Realtor.com data cited by CNBC.Cash purchases have also declined faster than the overall housing market. Total home sales fell 8.5% year-on-year during the period, while the number of cash sales dropped 11.2%.The shift comes as price growth has slowed sharply. The national median home price increased just 0.2% annually, compared with 1.8% growth in 2025 and a peak annual increase of 15.4% in 2021.âCash buyers arenât disappearing; theyâre simply becoming less dominant as the housing market finds its footing,â Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a release.âMore inventory and moderating prices are giving financed buyers more opportunities to compete,â she said, adding that cash continues to give sellers confidence that transactions can close quickly and with fewer surprises.Cash buyers lose ground after years of dominanceCash had gained importance during the pandemic-era housing boom, when limited supply and intense bidding wars made cash offers particularly attractive. Its importance continued after interest rates rose.But recent data indicate that trend is reversing.According to a National Association of Realtors survey cited by CNBC, cash accounted for 26% of existing-home sales in July 2026, down from 31% in July 2025.The decline has not been uniform across the country. Pittsburgh, Austin and San Francisco recorded increases in the share of transactions completed with cash compared with a year earlier.In those markets, the rise was also accompanied by an increase in the actual number of cash purchases.Financed buyers are winning competitive dealsDana Bull, a real estate agent in the Boston area, said she has seen fewer cash buyers even though the Boston market remains competitive.âThere was certainly a period of time when cash was king, which was right after interest rates climbed and aggressive bidding wars were commonplace. Itâs been tapering off,â Bull said, as quoted by CNBC.She said buyers are still waiving financing terms in some cases, while she recommends that clients in hotter neighbourhoods obtain pre-underwriting, rather than only pre-approval, to strengthen their offers against cash buyers.Bull cited two recent examples in which financed buyers won competitive bidding situations.âI had a client win a bidding war against about 15 offers this spring (financed with pre-underwriting), and my team member just beat out 27 other offers on a house in Arlington (also financed),â she said.âI donât think this would have happened in 2022-2025 during the cash craze,â Bull added.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: India, China could help Trump resolve Iran crisis through diplomacy: Hillary Clinton
articles.summary: US News: Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has said India and China could play a key role in helping resolve the escalating Iran crisis, urging Pres.
articles.body: Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has said India and China could play a key role in helping resolve the escalating Iran crisis, urging President Donald Trump to pursue âdiplomacy instead of blusterâ.In an interview with C-SPAN, Clinton said China and India could exert influence on Tehran because of their economic and energy ties with Iran.âIf you want to figure out how Trump could get out of this, I think the key to it is probably China and India, because if you look at who buys the most oil and gas from Iran, it's China and India,â Clinton said.India, China could pressure TehranClinton said China, in particular, could use its position as one of Iranâs biggest oil and gas buyers to pressure Tehran over the ongoing crisis.âChina is far ahead of that; they have been banking a lot of fossil fuels they got in tankers ... they have been building more reserves ... but they are going to need Iran,â she said.Clinton argued that economic leverage from countries such as China and India could offer Washington a diplomatic route to de-escalate the conflict.âIt does seem to me that's where the best pressure would come from if Trump were willing to actually use diplomacy instead of bluster,â she said.Strait of Hormuz remains key flashpointThe Strait of Hormuz remains at the centre of the crisis, with disruptions to shipping threatening a major global energy route. Nearly a fifth of the world's energy supplies passed through the Gulf chokepoint in normal times.Clinton said she would use the threat of secondary sanctions against China to push Beijing to persuade Iran to reopen the strategic waterway and restore the previous situation.âI would certainly tell the Chinese I was unless they were going to help us to try to get the Iranians to open the Strait of Hormuz and try to go back at least to the status quo ante,â she said.US steps up sanctions pressure on IranClinton's remarks came as the Trump administration intensified economic pressure on Tehran. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a fresh round of sanctions targeting Iran and warned countries doing business with the Islamic Republic to sever their financial ties or face US retaliation.Tehran has threatened to respond militarily to Washington's expanded sanctions, while Iran has also signalled willingness to resume talks.China, Turkiye and the UAE are among Iran's largest trading partners. Pakistan, Oman and Qatar have also been involved in efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran.Clinton, however, specifically identified India and China as countries that could help put pressure on Tehran because of their energy ties with Iran.Trump threatens 'crushing economic operation'The latest escalation follows Trump's August 20 warning that he would launch what he called the âmost crushing economic operationâ against Iran if Tehran failed to reach a deal.Clinton also criticised what she described as strategic miscalculations surrounding the conflict, saying the decisions that led to the current crisis had failed to deliver the political outcome Washington sought.She said greater involvement by countries with strong economic ties to Iran could provide an alternative to further military escalation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Mumbai builder told to pay Rs 6 crore to housing society over 20-year delay in occupation certificate
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) has directed a Mumbai builder to pay Rs 6 crore to a cooperative housing societ.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) has directed a Mumbai builder to pay Rs 6 crore to a cooperative housing society after finding that its members had been living under the continuing risk of demolition for more than 20 years because the developer failed to obtain an occupation certificate.The commission also directed the builder to obtain the occupation certificate within 12 months and pay Rs 10 lakh towards litigation costs. The judgment was pronounced on August 17, 2026.What was the dispute over the housing society's redevelopment?As per the commission order, Tirupati Devi Cooperative Housing Society, comprising 33 members occupying 25 flats in two wings of Balaji Apartments in Santa Cruz, had entered into a redevelopment agreement with Raja Construction Company on March 14, 2005. Under the agreement, the developer was required to demolish the old buildings, construct new ones and provide flats to the existing members. The developer was also responsible for obtaining the occupation certificate and new water connection.The developer handed over possession of the flats from 2008 onwards. However, the society alleged that it failed to provide the sanctioned building plans, occupation certificate, completion certificate and new water connections.After an RTI application, the members allegedly came to know that the construction did not match the sanctioned plans. The society further alleged that additional construction had been carried out and because of the same the authority denied granting the occupation certificate.The society approached the NCDRC in 2013 seeking compensation for the delay, differences in the flat areas, regularisation charges and the failure to provide the required certificates. However, the builder denied the allegations and argued that the complaint was filed late. It also claimed that some of the flat owners had themselves made illegal changes to their flats and because of that the the occupation certificate was not issued.The commission, however, found that there was no evidence supporting the builder's claim that the members had carried out illegal construction. It noted that the developer had itself agreed to provide the additional carpet area and had undertaken responsibility for obtaining the occupation certificate and completing the necessary formalities.What did the commission say while holding the builder responsible?The bench comprising President A.P. Sahi and member Bharatkumar Pandya, noted that although the members had received possession of their flats in 2008, the legality of the construction remained in doubt because the construction was in excess of or contrary to the approved plans. It also found that the developer had taken the risk of constructing additional area and had failed to obtain the required approvals.âThough the possession is being enjoyed by the members from 2008 onwards, the legality of the extent of construction and of such possession is in jeopardy in view of the refusal or resistance by the authorities to grant such permission in view of the fact of part of the construction being in excess of or contrary to the approved plan as submitted by the Developer to the authorities,â the commission said.The commission further rejected the builder's argument that the society members were responsible for the problem. It said the developer had the responsibility of preparing proper plans, carrying out construction according to those plans and obtaining the occupation certificate.âThere is no evidence on record and no merit in the contention of the OP that the members have made any illegal construction in their units. It is the OP who promised, constructed and handed over the flats with 20 percent additional carpet area to the original members,â it further added.The commission held that the absence of the occupation certificate had become a continuing problem for the society and its members. It noted that they had been facing anxiety and the risk of demolition for more than 20 years.âIn our considered opinion, the non-obtaining of the OC and putting the members under the continuing risk of demolition of the building due to illegality in construction over a longish period of more than 20 years, calls for the compensation at enhanced 1.5 times the stipulated rate, which would be just and fair and would duly take care of the anxiety and mental agony and adversity faced and being faced by the society and its members,â the bench noted.The commission noted that the redevelopment agreement itself provided for compensation of Rs 1 lakh per month if the developer failed to complete the project within 24 months. However, considering the long delay and the continuing risk faced by the members, it increased the compensation rate to 1.5 times that amount for the period from June 2008 to August 2026. This worked out to Rs 3.24 crore, after which the commission added another Rs 26 lakh for the additional hardship and expenses caused by the absence of municipal water connection and additional municipal taxes.The commission then awarded a further Rs 2.5 crore, taking the total compensation to Rs 6 crore. It said the members had been living under a continuing threat of demolition because the occupation certificate had still not been obtained.The builder and its partners were held jointly and severally responsible for the deficiency in service. The commission directed them to pay the Rs 6 crore compensation within three months. If they failed to pay, the amount would carry 8 percent simple interest until full payment.The commission also directed the builder to pay all necessary charges and obtain the occupation certificate within 12 months, and hand it over to the society and its 33 current members. It further directed the builder to pay Rs 10 lakh towards litigation costs within three months.

articles.title: Plastic nurdles wash up on Hartlepool and North Yorkshire beaches
articles.summary: Plastic nurdles are washing up on beaches more than 30 miles south of the Port of Tyne spill site.
articles.body:
Nurdles are washing up on beaches more than 30 miles (48km) south of the source of a spillage of millions of plastic pellets.

Tonnes of the pieces of plastic, known as nurdles, washed up across north-east England after a crash between two vessels at the Port of Tyne damaged two shipping containers.

The nurdles have now been spotted on beaches in North Yorkshire and Teesside, and volunteers are worried the clean-up effort is being "left to communities" and called for a "long-term plan".

The Port of Tyne said its response had not been "scaled back" and it continued to maintain the same level of on-water resource as throughout the clean-up operation.

The port said during the recent high tide period it had temporarily increased the number of boats and operatives deployed.

North East mayor Kim McGuinness said her team had contacted Solis Marine, the company organising the clean-up on behalf of the shipping insurers, to ask them to commit to responding to new nurdle deposits and asking why casual workers had been stood down.

She said: "They should not be allowed to decide on their own what a proper clean-up looks like.

"Our local volunteers have given up their time and worn themselves out combing beaches."

Solis Marine has been approached for comment and a Port of Tyne spokesperson said the response continued to be guided by Ambipar, experts in environmental spill response.

"We remain committed to removing as much material from the river as possible within that expert guidance," they said.

Environmental charity Fidra, which runs the Great Nurdle Hunt project, said nurdles were highly mobile and they would continue to wash up in the north-east of England and beyond in the months and years to come.

A spokesperson said: "There needs to be a long-term plan and resources to monitor and respond when nurdles wash up in the future.

"The continued spread of nurdles to regions far from the source of the spill vividly highlights the wide reaching impact - volunteers are reporting new finds every day."

The charity called for regulation and international maritime organisation rules for pellet loss prevention and preparedness plans.

Redcar and Cleveland Borough Council officers have inspected beaches from Marske to Redcar and confirmed nurdles had been found.

Currently, the authority said they were "concentrated in relatively small pockets".

"Teams are also looking to organise targeted beach clearance days, where volunteers can support the clean-up effort," a spokesperson said.

"In addition, we are exploring the use of appropriate mechanical equipment to help expedite the removal process, where this can be undertaken safely and without causing damage to the coastline or sensitive habitats."

Senior scientist at the National Oceanography Centre Dr Charlotte Williams said tides were highly predictable and tidal currents generally move water back and forth.

"Floating material such as nurdles would be transported by a combination of processes, including tides, winds, waves and larger-scale coastal currents," she said.

"Wind, and the surface currents can be really variable and are often more important for moving floating material than the back-and-forth motion of the tide alone."

Durham County Council confirmed its officers had been carrying out daily patrols along the coast and "a very small number" of pellets were found on Monday morning.

Head of environment for the county council, James Gilchrist, said: "We will continue to monitor the situation alongside partner agencies and should there be a need for a clean-up that volunteers can take part in, we will publicise details of this."

articles.title: Indian-origin former Optum director sentenced to 3 years in prison over $950,000 fraud scheme
articles.summary: US News: Karan Gupta, an Indian-origin former director at Optum, has been sentenced to three years in prison for a $950,000 fraud scheme involving no-show jobs and kickbacks. Gupta's actions impacted a healthcare provider serving millions of Americans.
articles.body: An Indian-origin former director at healthcare company Optum has been sentenced to three years in prison for his role in a scheme that defrauded the company of more than $950,000.Karan Gupta, 48, based in California, was sentenced on August 24 after being convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, 10 counts of wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering,according to the US Attorney's Office for Minnesota.Gupta, who served as a senior director at Optum, was found guilty by a federal jury on February 17 following a six-day trial.According to court documents, Gupta arranged a no-show job for his longtime friend, Shangraf Kaul, 45, of East Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania.Gupta hired Kaul as a data engineering manager on his team in late 2015, despite Kaul allegedly lacking the qualifications for the position. Prosecutors said Kaul performed no work at Optum for more than three years while receiving a six-figure salary.Gupta allegedly demanded that Kaul return about 60% of his salary as kickbacks. The payments were initially made through cash deposits into Gupta's bank account before the pair used a separate checking account that Gupta could access to conceal the money transfers.The scheme was uncovered after Optum terminated Gupta in November 2019 over his involvement in a similar no-show employee fraud. The company investigated the matter and referred it to federal law enforcement.US Attorney Daniel N. Rosen said the fraud affected more than just the company.âDefrauding a private company is not a victimless crime,â Rosen said, adding that Gupta's actions undermined a healthcare provider relied upon by millions of Americans.Gupta's co-conspirator, Kaul, pleaded guilty in February 2025 to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Rhode Island woman bought her familyâs coastal farm in 1908, spent decades painting and birdwatching there, then left the land to become a sanctuary that now protects 300 acres
articles.summary: US News: Mabel Norman Cerio spent much of her life between art and nature at Paradise Farm in Middletown, Rhode Island. In 1908, she bought the coastal propert.
articles.body: Mabel Norman Cerio spent much of her life between art and nature at Paradise Farm in Middletown, Rhode Island. In 1908, she bought the coastal property from the estate of her brother after the death of her father. Decades later, the land would become the Norman Bird Sanctuary, a protected space covering 300 acres.Cerio was a lifelong lover of art and nature. After making Paradise Farm her home and studio, she spent years painting, caring for animals and birdwatching on the property. Her interest in conservation also grew during this period. According to Newport Historical Society, soon after buying the farm, she began making plans for a bird sanctuary and wildlife refuge.Cerio died in 1949. Through her trust, she left Paradise Farm to the community for the purpose of creating a sanctuary. The property was named the Norman Bird Sanctuary after her father and her late brother, George H Norman Jr. The organisation was formally established in 1949 through her bequest.Today, the Norman Bird Sanctuary is the steward of the largest contiguous open space on Aquidneck Island. It protects 300 acres of diverse habitat and has six miles of hiking trails. Its work includes wildlife conservation, habitat restoration and environmental education.Making of a wildlife sanctuaryParadise Farm had been part of the Norman family's property before Cerio bought it. The Cultural Landscape Foundation records that the historic coastal farm had a farmhouse built, with later additions, around 1750. The land had been used for sheep grazing, mixed crops and salt marsh hay, and had passed through several owners.In the late 19th century, Newport businessman George Norman acquired the property to secure water rights for the Newport Water Works. After his death in 1900, the farm was inherited by Mabel's older brother Guy. Cerio later purchased it from him in 1908 and made the estate her home and studio.Her decision to preserve the property was not simply about keeping the family land. According to the Newport Historical Society, the sanctuary's work today reflects that early interest in conservation.Mabel's life as an artistWhile Cerio is now best known for the sanctuary, records from the Newport Historical Society show that art was another major part of her life.Born in Newport in 1876, Cerio spent her early years at the family's Belair estate before continuing her education away from home.She became a dedicated artist, with painting as her main medium. Seven of her portraits were displayed at the Panama-Pacific exhibition in 1915. She also explored sculpture, according to correspondence preserved by the Newport Historical Society.Some of the records that shed light on this side of her life come from Hendrik Christian Andersen, a Norwegian-born artist who settled in Italy. Between May 1911 and September 1912, Andersen sent Cerio 35 postcards, 11 short letters and four notes on calling cards while she was living at 25 Via Gregoriana in Rome.His correspondence shows that the two had a close personal and professional relationship. Andersen regularly asked about Cerio's painting and offered advice about her artistic work. His letters also indicate that she was experimenting with sculpture.A lasting legacyThe land Cerio left behind has continued to serve the purpose she envisioned. The Norman Bird Sanctuary now protects diverse habitats and provides space for wildlife, visitors and educational programmes.The sanctuary says its mission is to encourage people to explore nature, care for it and find peace and joy in it. Its 300 acres include open spaces and wildlife habitat, while its trails provide access across the property.The landscape includes open fields, wetlands and woodlands. Historic features of the original farm remain, including fieldstone walls, parts of an orchard, a garden, a stone-lined sheep pen and an abandoned quarry. Hanging Rock, an outcropping represented in paintings and photographs, is also part of the landscape.The original farmstead was designated the Smith-Gardiner-Norman Farm Historic District and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2008.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: A look back at Dolly Parton’s life and accomplishments.
articles.body: A look back at Dolly Parton’s life and accomplishments. Sen. Darline Graham wins the GOP primary runoff for her late brother’s Senate seat. And NASA’s new telescope could change our understanding of the universe. Here’s what to know today. Dolly Parton, country music icon, dies at 80 Dolly Parton, who rose from a loving but impoverished upbringing in the mountains of East Tennessee to become the “Queen of Country” music, a Hollywood star and a beloved American icon, has died at 80. Her team said she had battled cancer briefly and died Tuesday surrounded by her loved ones. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Accolades quickly poured in from friends and fellow entertainers, from Reba McEntire and Dione Warwick to the Muppets and Donatella Versace. President Donald Trump ordered flags lowered for a week. See the tributes to Parton. The outpouring of praise for the larger-than-life superstar from politicians on both sides of the aisle and celebrities underscored how she transcended cultural, political, geographic and generational divides. Parton endeared herself to the red and the blue, the heartland and the coasts, even as the monoculture splintered and political polarization turned friends into strangers. Why Parton was universally beloved. During her more than 60-year career, Parton sold over 100 million records and won 11 Grammy Awards, with hits like “Jolene,” “I Will Always Love You” and “Here You Come Again.” She also became a star on the silver screen in movies like “9 to 5,” “Steel Magnolias” and “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas.” See her life in photos. Parton presided over an entertainment empire that included the Dollywood theme park. Her philanthropic legacy includes the creation of the Imagination Library, which mails free books to children around the world and was inspired by her father, who was illiterate. The strikes have forced Congress to find billions of dollars to repair the facilities and prompted officials to reconsider how to deploy personnel and intelligence resources in a region facing an elevated threat from Tehran’s growing drone and missile arsenal, two of the people said. The CIA has offices on U.S. embassy compounds in more than a dozen countries across the Middle East. NASA telescope could transform our view of the cosmos A new NASA observatory set to launch into space this weekend is poised to survey more of the cosmos than any telescope before it. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a bus-sized observatory and successor to the iconic Hubble Space Telescope, is scheduled to launch Sunday morning from Florida aboard a SpaceX rocket. It will then travel roughly 1 million miles from Earth to its destination. articles.title: German airport worker dies of malaria after 'mosquito arrives on plane'
articles.summary: Five other airport workers are also receiving treatment following the rare outbreak at German's busiest airport.
articles.body:
A Frankfurt Airport worker has died of malaria after a rare outbreak led to six employees contracting the serious infection spread by mosquitoes.

It is believed the mosquitoes arrived at Germany's busiest airport on a plane, according to German public health officials.

The remaining five infected individuals are receiving medical treatment, a spokesperson for airport operator Fraport said.

Traps have been installed at the airport and mosquitoes captured will be analysed in a laboratory to determine their species and origin.

"Sadly, we must confirm that one employee has died as a result of the infection," the Fraport spokesperson told the BBC.

"We have provided comprehensive information to all employees and encourage them to consult a doctor if they experience any symptoms."

It was reported in July that the outbreak involved four infected workers.

The Robert Koch Institute - a German federal government agency and research institute for disease control and public health - previously said the four employees fell ill between 4 and 6 July and the mosquitoes were brought in by plane.

The institute said malaria in Germany almost exclusively affects long-haul travellers who were infected in malaria-endemic areas, and that malaria transmitted within a German airport is rare.

"The lack of a travel history can lead to a delayed diagnosis. A delayed diagnosis increases the risk of a severe course of the diseases," the institute said in its epidemiological bulletin.

The last case of airport malaria was in 2023 also at Frankfurt Airport, it added.

The BBC has contacted Frankfurt Public Health Department, who is leading the investigation into the outbreak, for comment.

Malaria is a disease spread by some types of mosquitoes biting humans, and is mostly found in tropical countries, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The infection, which is preventable and curable, is caused by a parasite and does not spread from person to person. However symptoms can be mild or life-threatening.

articles.title: Middlesbrough murder investigation as two people die in house fire
articles.summary: Cleveland Police says it "cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime" after the fire near Middlesbrough.
articles.body:
A murder investigation has been launched after two people died in a house fire.

The blaze in Grangetown, Middlesbrough, broke out just before 05:30 BST and also left a woman in hospital in a critical condition, alongside a further three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Cleveland Police said it was investigating what had happened but was "keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

The fire happened about two miles from the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers on Saturday morning.

Redcar and Cleveland Local Policing Commander Supt Emily Harrison said the force was working to "establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened".

"We will have a high visibility presence in the Grangetown area as this investigation progresses, and to provide reassurance to local communities, who will no doubt be impacted by this tragic incident."

Patrols have been increased in the local area to "reassure the local community", the force said.

Firefighters damped down the smoking roof of the home which has been wrecked by the fire.

A ladder was propped against a rear upstairs window of the family home.

A neighbour, who asked not to be named, said: "My daughter heard shouting and screaming this morning.

The neighbour said a family lived at the house, adding: "I don't know the people who live there, we just say hello when we walk past."

Police officers guarded a cordon around the scene and Northern Powergrid staff were also on site.

Cleveland Fire Brigade said it sent six fire engines and the Incident Command Unit to the scene.

A spokesperson said road closures were in place in the surrounding area and asked members of the public to avoid the area where possible.

Redcar MP Anna Turley said the community had faced a "profound amount of heartbreak over the past few weeks".

She said: "I am devastated to hear of the tragic loss of life following this morning's fire in Grangetown.

"My deepest condolences are with the families, friends and loved ones of those who have died, and my thoughts are also with those injured and receiving treatment."

Grangetown councillor Adam Brook urged people not to speculate.

He said: "Many residents have been in touch with me throughout the morning, and I know there is understandably a great deal of concern.

"However, I would urge people not to speculate or share unconfirmed information."

The families of the people involved have been informed and they are being supported by specialist officers.

articles.title: In the 1970s, Britain imported North American signal crayfish for farms; they escaped, bred in huge numbers and now infest rivers across England, Wales and Scotland, carrying a plague deadly to native crayfish
articles.summary: UK News: In the 1970s, British aquaculture businesses imported North American signal crayfish to stock farms, hoping to build a profitable new freshwater fishe.
articles.body: In the 1970s, British aquaculture businesses imported North American signal crayfish to stock farms, hoping to build a profitable new freshwater fishery. But the plan backfired: the hardy invaders escaped into rivers, multiplied rapidly and spread across England, Wales and Scotland. Today they dominate many waterways and carry crayfish plague, a disease that is usually fatal to the UKâs only native crayfish, the white-clawed species. The UK Government documents describe signal crayfish as a textbook case of how non-native species can damage biodiversity, out-compete natives and alter river ecosystems. This story is based on UK government policy reports and recent Environment Agency reporting on native crayfish conservation. Read on to know more:How signal crayfish arrived, and why they spread so fastSignal crayfish (Pacifastacus leniusculus) were brought into the UK from North America in the 1970s for farming, intended as a commercial species for restaurants and local markets. They are larger, faster-growing and more aggressive than the native white-clawed crayfish (Austropotamobius pallipes), giving them an immediate advantage in competition for food and shelter.Once they escaped from farms into the wild, they proved exceptionally good at colonising new habitats. They breed in large numbers, tolerate a wide range of water conditions and can move through connected river systems with relative ease. Over the decades, they have established populations in rivers and streams across much of England, Wales and Scotland, turning what began as a controlled aquaculture experiment into a widespread invasive-species problem.The hidden weapon: crayfish plagueThe most damaging aspect of the signal crayfish invasion is not just competition: itâs disease. Signal crayfish carry crayfish plague, a waterborne pathogen caused by the oomycete Aphanomyces astaci. The disease rarely harms signal crayfish themselves, but it is usually lethal to white-clawed crayfish, which have no natural immunity.When signal crayfish move into a river system that holds native populations, they can trigger mass die-offs.The plague spreads through the water and via contaminated equipment, clothing and boats, making it hard to contain once established. This dynamic has pushed the white-clawed crayfish toward local extinctions in many catchments and contributed to its status as an endangered species in the UK.Impact on rivers, banks and other wildlifeSignal crayfish do far more than crowd out native species; they tear apart whole river ecosystems. As they dig burrows into riverbanks, they weaken the soil and trigger severe erosion in small streams and ditches. Their relentless appetite makes things worse. By devouring fish eggs and aquatic bugs, they starve local wildlife and unravel complex food webs. Once these aggressive generalists take over, rich, diverse waters degrade into simplified systems dominated by a single pest. Protecting our native crayfish is about more than saving one creature. It is about keeping entire freshwater habitats healthy and resilient.A recent scare and glimmers of hope for native crayfishThe vulnerability of native populations was underscored in autumn 2024 when some 100 white-clawed crayfish were found dead in the River Wansbeck catchment in Northumberland, a nationally important stronghold for the species. Surveys in summer 2025 revealed that many affected crayfish had unusual orange patches and ulcers on their shells, but the symptoms didnât appear to be fatal at the population level. Investigations by the Environment Agency, the National Trust and university researchers found that some crayfish, especially younger individuals, could recover through normal moulting, and that mortality seemed concentrated in older, larger animals. No further deaths were reported after autumn 2024, and the Wansbeck population is still considered a key refuge for the species. Importantly, no signal crayfish are known from the Wansbeck catchment, and crayfish plague was ruled out as the cause of those particular mortalities.What the government is doing, and what the public can doUK policy explicitly recognises signal crayfish as a non-native species that has âcaused troubleâ for native wildlife, and uses it as a case study for why stricter controls on importing and moving live aquatic species are necessary.Regulations now require risk assessments for new species introductions and govern the movement of live fish and crayfish between water bodies to reduce disease spread.Conservation efforts focus on creating âark sitesâ, isolated water bodies where white-clawed crayfish can live and breed without exposure to signal crayfish or plague. After the 2024 incident, healthy âberriedâ females were rescued from the Wansbeck, their eggs hatched in captivity, and the offspring are being released into ark sites to bolster populations.For river users, the advice is simple but critical: Check, Clean, Dry.Check clothing and equipment for mud, aquatic animals or plant material and remove anything found.Clean everything thoroughly as soon as possible, using hot water where feasible.Dry for at least 48 hours, or use a suitable disinfectant before using gear elsewhere.Anyone who sees crayfish, alive or dead, is urged to leave them in place and report sightings to the Environment Agency, as it is illegal to handle or remove crayfish without the correct licences.A cautionary tale for invasive species policyThe story of signal crayfish in the UK is a clear example of how short-term economic decisions can create long-term ecological costs. What began as a promising aquaculture venture in the 1970s has become a persistent threat to native biodiversity, riverbank stability and the future of the white-clawed crayfish.Today, the focus is on containment, conservation and public awareness: protecting remaining strongholds, expanding ark sites and ensuring that people who enjoy rivers and lakes understand their role in preventing further spread. For policymakers, the signal crayfish episode underpins stricter rules on non-native species and reinforces the principle that preventing introductions is far easier, and cheaper, than trying to reverse them once they take hold.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: From Kanganaâs âbikiniâ barb to GIVA pulling ad: How Kriti Sanonâs Raksha Bandhan row unfolded
articles.summary: MUMBAI: A jewellery advertisement featuring actor Kriti Sanon ahead of Raksha Bandhan has snowballed into a wider debate over clothing, culture and wo.
articles.body: MUMBAI: A jewellery advertisement featuring actor Kriti Sanon ahead of Raksha Bandhan has snowballed into a wider debate over clothing, culture and womenâs freedom.The advertisement soon drew criticism from BJP MP Kangana Ranaut, a response from Sanon, backing from Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and, finally, the withdrawal of the campaign by jewellery brand GIVA.The controversy centred on GIVAâs Raksha Bandhan campaign featuring Sanon in an Indo-Western outfit comprising a bralette-style blouse, cape and draped skirt.While the advertisement was intended as a festive campaign, its styling triggered criticism online.Some social media users questioned whether Sanonâs outfit was appropriate for a Raksha Bandhan advertisement and also pointed to the absence of traditional elements associated with the festival.Kanganaâs âbikiniâ remark sparks rowThe controversy gained momentum after actor-turned-politician Kangana Ranaut aimed the advertisement in an Instagram Story.Ranaut questioned why a woman would tie a Rakhi while wearing what she described as a bikini or undergarments, arguing that women today have a wide range of clothing options.âItâs a wonderful time to be a woman. Our closets are full of a variety of clothes; todayâs woman is a global woman,â Kangana wrote.She went on to list options ranging from cocktail dresses and lehenga cholis to jeans, saris, bikinis and salwar kameez, before asking why one would choose such an outfit while tying a Rakhi.Calling the advertisement âintentionally creepyâ, Ranaut questioned the way the festival had been portrayed.The criticism added fuel to an already active online debate, with some users also questioning why traditional elements such as a puja thali and tilak were absent from the campaign.âCulture & traditions are in her heart, not her necklineâ: Kriti hits backSanon subsequently responded to the criticism, though she did not name Ranaut directly.In an Instagram post, the actor said the essence of a festival was not determined by the clothes a person wore but by the emotions and meaning attached to the tradition.She described Raksha Bandhan as a bond of protection and said she and her sister tie Rakhi to each other, adding that they pray for each otherâs âhealth, happiness & long lifeâ.Sanon also explained that the same sentiment extended to their dogs, whom they considered family.The actor then broadened her response beyond the advertisement itself, questioning why women continued to be told what to wear.She said ethnic fashion had evolved, but a womanâs respect for her culture was still being judged by her clothes.Her post ended with the line, âCulture & Traditions are in her heart, not her neckline!âRahul Gandhi enters debateThe controversy then took a political turn after the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, came out in Sanonâs support.Gandhi said a womanâs clothing, actions and movements were her own choices and urged people to stop trolling women for exercising their freedom.âWhat a woman wears, what she does and where she goes - is her choice,â Gandhi said in an Instagram post. âStop trolling women for exercising their freedom.âHis intervention shifted the conversation further from the advertisementâs styling to the broader question of whether womenâs clothing should be used as a measure of their cultural values.GIVA pulls advertisementAs the controversy continued, GIVA announced that it had withdrawn the advertisement from all media.In a statement shared on Instagram, the jewellery brand said it had the âhighest regard and deep respectâ for Indian culture, traditions and festivals.The company said it had intended to celebrate the festive occasion with families and had sought to extend that celebration to pets as well.GIVA said that if the advertisement had inadvertently hurt the sentiments of some sections of society, that was never its intention.âOut of respect, we have withdrawn the said advertisement from all media,â the brand said.It concluded its statement by wishing people âlove & positivityâ during the festive season.A festive ad turns into a larger debateThe episode has since moved beyond the advertisement itself.The exchange between Kangana and Sanon has opened up a larger debate over how women dress during festivals, who gets to define cultural appropriateness and whether clothing can be used to judge a woman's respect for tradition.What began as a festive jewellery campaign eventually turned into a public debate involving actors, politicians and the brand itself.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Singapore will pay about $55,000 in support for each child; why the country is paying parents to have babies
articles.summary: World News: Singapore has a problem that money alone has not been able to solve. People there are having fewer children. Now the country is trying a bigger, longe.
articles.body: Singapore has a problem that money alone has not been able to solve. People there are having fewer children. Now the country is trying a bigger, longer-term approach. Singapore will provide almost S$70,000 (around US$55,000 or roughly Rs 47 lakh) in direct financial support for every Singaporean child, from birth until the child turns 17.The announcement was made by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong during Singapore's National Day Rally on August 23. But the headline figure needs some context. This is not a S$70,000 cheque that parents receive after having a baby. The amount is spread across different forms of support, including cash payments, healthcare-related grants, child credits and education support.The move comes as Singapore's fertility rate has fallen to its lowest recorded level. According to Singapore's Department of Statistics, the country's resident total fertility rate fell from 0.97 in 2024 to just 0.87 in 2025. There were 29,864 live births in 2025, down 11.4% from the previous year.The numbers explain why the government is trying something different.The money will follow the child, not just the birthSingapore already has one of Asia's better-known fertility-support systems, including its Baby Bonus Scheme. But the new SG Child Support Package changes the way that assistance is structured.According to Channel NewsAsia and various media, the new package will replace the existing Baby Bonus Scheme and Large Families Scheme. Unlike the current system, the new package will provide the same baseline level of support for every Singaporean child, regardless of birth order.The support will also last longer. At present, much of the Baby Bonus support is concentrated in a child's early years. Under the new package, assistance will continue until the child turns 17.Starting April 1, 2027, each eligible newborn will receive a S$10,000 cash gift, paid in two installments within the first year.There will also be S$5,000 deposited into the child's Child Development Account, another S$5,000 in government co-matching of parents' CDA savings, S$2,000 in Child Credits every year for the first 16 years, a S$10,000 top-up to the Post-Secondary Education Account at age 17. Put together, these benefits bring the government's direct support to almost S$70,000 per child.Why Singapore is doing this nowSingapore's fertility rate has been falling for years despite repeated government efforts to encourage marriage and parenthood. The latest number 0.87 children per woman in 2025 is far below the roughly 2.1 level generally associated with population replacement in the absence of migration.This is not just about the number of babies being born. Fewer births today mean a smaller working-age population in the future, while longer life expectancy means more older people needing care and support. That creates pressure on everything from the workforce and healthcare to pensions, housing and the tax base.Singapore's government has therefore been looking at parenthood as a long-term national issue rather than simply a personal choice.The government knows money cannot solve everythingInterestingly, Prime Minister Wong did not suggest that a bigger payment would automatically make people have more children. In a recent speech, Wong acknowledged that the decision to have children is deeply personal and that government policies alone cannot make it happen. The aim, he said, is to make it easier for people who already want children to start and raise a family.The new package is not only about money. Singapore is also expanding support for parents who need time away from work to look after their children. The government has said it will take on a greater share of the cost of expanded childcare leave, reducing the burden on employers.There is another notable change. Under the existing Baby Bonus structure, some benefits are linked to the parents being lawfully married. The new SG Child Support Package will extend its benefits to all Singaporean children, regardless of their parents' marital status or family circumstances.So will S$70,000 actually make people have more babies?The government can make childcare cheaper. It can provide cash. It can support education. It can offer parents more leave and make housing easier to access. What it cannot do is make people want children. And that may be the hardest part of the problem Singapore is trying to solve.For now, the country is betting that if the financial and practical burden becomes lighter, at least some couples who are already thinking about having children may decide that the time is right.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK days after announcing move
articles.summary: Prince Harry, Meghan, and their two children are believed to have flown into the country privately from California.
articles.body:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived back in the UK, BBC News understands.

Prince Harry, Meghan and their children Archie and Lilibet are believed to have flown into the country privately from California, and landed in Birmingham shortly before midday.

A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said "this is not something we would comment on".

There did not appear to be a police presence as Harry and his family left the airport, a source told the BBC.

Last week, it was reported that the couple would be relocating to the UK in August. They will not return to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals.

It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in school and the new term is due to start next week.

The Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties in early 2020, before settling in California in March that year.

King Charles was told of the move earlier this month. The family visited the King at his Highgrove home in July this year, but it is understood the move was not discussed.

Before that visit, Prince Harry and Meghan had not been in the UK together since they attended the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II in 2022.

Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?

The Prince and Princess of Wales have also been informed of their plans.

The Sussexes' security in the UK has been the subject of debate since the news of their return broke.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the country.

The duke had sought to overturn a decision that had downgraded his security after he stopped being a working royal and moved to the US.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security in the UK and who will pay for it.

After the announcement of the Sussexes' intended return, a Home Office spokesperson said decisions on the security of royals were taken by the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures (Ravec), and the UK government's protective security system was "rigorous and proportionate".

Prince Harry has previously said that worries about safety have prevented him from coming to the UK and bringing his wife and children.

Last month, the duke and six other public figures lost their High Court privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail and Mail.

They face paying up to £34.5m to Associated Newspapers in legal costs.

articles.title: 9 common myths about wrinkles debunked — and what dermatologists want you to know instead
articles.summary: From the importance of genetics to whether $200 moisturizers are a good buy, here's the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

I once read about a lady who didn't smile for over 40 years . Her reason for such a stationary expression was not a distaste for joy and laughter, but something else entirely — to prevent wrinkles . She'd decided that maintaining a straight, expressionless face was worth it to keep smooth, youthful-looking skin. (Apparently, she even resisted smiling when her daughter was born! Can you imagine?)

Sometimes, when I'm slathering on my lotions and potions in the evening, I think about this woman. Not because it's a cautionary tale about vanity, but because her fear wasn't necessarily directed at the right thing. Wrinkle mythology is full of misplaced fears and misplaced faith. We treat certain habits like miracle workers and others like poison, often with evidence pointed in the opposite direction. So, instead of guessing what to do and what to avoid, I asked dermatologists to bust some wrinkle myths and misconceptions. (But as the great Oscar Wilde once said, "The truth is rarely pure and never simple.")

Myth #1: Facial expressions are the main cause of wrinkles

Let's address the aforementioned smile-averse situation. If we stop facial movement, whether it's a smile, frown or Elvis-like lip snarl, it would stop wrinkles, right? According to Dr. Behrooz Torkian , a double board-certified facial plastic surgeon based in Beverly Hills, Calif., it's not that simple. Now, some wrinkles really are caused by movement: "A prime example of this is the wrinkles on the forehead, the glabella, or so-called 'elevens,' and the crow's feet," he says. But movement is also competing with bigger forces like sun exposure and collagen loss. His advice is to limit repetitive movement with Botox where it matters, and protect collagen with adequate SPF , a good diet, stress control and no smoking.

To rebuild collagen, Torkian recommends vitamin C , retinoids , growth factors and peptides , along with regular microneedling, radio frequency and laser treatments. And if you happen to have a red light mask in your closet, now's the time to break it out. "Recent scientific evidence on red light therapy has also supported the use of red and near-infrared light to support the metabolic processes of building collagen in the skin," he says.

Myth #2: How much you wrinkle depends solely on genetics

Your bloodline may set things up for your skin, but it doesn't decide the outcome alone. "Genetics matter because your genes shape how thick your skin is, how well you hold onto collagen and how much melanin you have doing built-in sun protection," says Dr. Geeta Yadav, a board-certified dermatologist and founder of Facet Dermatology. This is part of why some people "start creasing in their 30s while others sail into their 60s looking smooth."

However, she points out how identical twins with identical DNA can look years apart in age. She underscores the sun's impact on our skin, which makes movement seem like a minor threat by comparison. "Sun alone is estimated to account for around 80% of the visible aging we see on the face," she says.

Myth #3: The more expensive the moisturizer, the better

By now, you probably know that drugstore beauty can go toe-to-toe with luxury brands , and moisture is no exception. "I have always believed that paying a lot for a moisturizer is not worth it," says Torkian. What matters, he says, is what's actually in the jar. Moisturizers break down into three parts: humectants that draw in water, emollients that soften and occlusives that seal it all in. Beyond that, you want to consider whether it has actives, such as peptides, retinoids, hydroxy acids and niacinamide. "As a general rule, I personally avoid the super expensive and the super cheap," he says.

Myth #4: Dry skin causes wrinkles; oily skin ages better

"One of the most essential factors in the appearance of wrinkles in skin is the hydration of the collagen, hyaluronic acid and elastin within the dermis and epidermis," explains Torkian. Oil definitely supports it, as more sebaceous glands mean the skin has a built-in defense system against losing that moisture. However, dry skin doesn't necessarily mean you're doomed. It just needs that same protection in a different way: "Moisturizers such as ceramides to augment the skin barrier" versus retinoids and hydroxy acids for oily skin — at least as a starting point.

According to Torkian, internal hydration is definitely a part of the picture, but only if the skin barrier is already intact and topical moisture is in place. But water alone doesn't do the plumping. A 2015 study published in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology showed that adding roughly 2 liters of water a day to women's diets for a month significantly improved skin hydration and biomechanics.

Ultimately, it's less that water plumps wrinkles and more that dehydration accelerates them. Yadav is more blunt, saying that drinking more water is unlikely to meaningfully change wrinkles.

Myth #6: Retinol and tretinoin are interchangeable

Both retinol and tretinoin speed up cell turnover and rebuild collagen, which smooths and softens wrinkles over time. But the real question is which one gets you there and how fast. Torkian breaks down how tretinoin is the active compound itself, whereas retinol has to go through two steps to convert into tretinoin. "This means that using tretinoin can lead to quicker results and quicker onset of the results, but it can also feel a little bit more harsh to skin that has not adjusted to retinoic acid yet," he says. Over the long term, results from both can be very similar, he adds.

Myth #7: Only in-office procedures can reverse wrinkles, not topicals

According to Torkian, the answer to this isn't a flat no. "There are some topicals that can be very helpful in reversing wrinkling," he says, "provided that the wrinkling has not gone out of hand." Retinoids, especially prescription tretinoin, have decades of trial evidence behind them, while vitamin C, growth factors and peptides can also make a difference.

But he doesn't stop there: "Another essential factor is whether proper prevention is being employed at the same time as using the topical that is intended to reverse wrinkling." In other words, a product working solo, without sun protection or consistency, applied to wrinkles that are already deeply set isn't a fair test of what topicals can actually do.

Myth #8: The neck and chest age faster than the face

While it's true that the skin on the neck and chest is very different from the skin on the face (mainly because there are fewer oil glands), Torkian pushes back on the framing of this myth, and points out the impact of our behavior. "One thing to keep in mind about the skin of the neck and chest is that they rarely get any love," he says. "I always like to remind my patients that when they have their skin-care routine, they should not forget the neck and chest. It is natural to want to use all of your expensive skin-care products on what you feel people are looking at the most, but spreading a little love below the chin can be impactful over time in preventing neck and chest aging."

Myth #9: Botox is the best treatment for all kinds of wrinkles

Yadav is clear that Botox is excellent for softening the dynamic lines caused by repeated muscle movement. "Frown lines, forehead lines and crow's feet respond beautifully, because quieting the muscle stops it folding the skin above it thousands of times a day," she explains. But it does much less for lines already etched in when your face is completely at rest, and very little for crepey texture, sun damage or the sagging that comes from lost volume and laxity, she says.

At under $10, this effective cream is proof of Myth #3 — you don't have to splurge to get real results. It pairs retinol with bakuchiol, a plant-derived retinol alternative that helps soften irritation, plus vitamin E and allantoin to keep skin calm. You get softer-looking lines and plumper, less flakey skin without the retinol redness.

One of the most effective anti-aging treatments available without a prescription is Differin. This dermatologist favorite can help improve skin texture, fine lines and overall skin tone as long as you're consistent. It can also help build collagen, which, in turn, makes skin look brighter and bouncier.

This budget-friendly moisturizer does barrier-repair work while you sleep thanks to a powerful trio of ceramides, hyaluronic acid and peptides. It's essentially the ingredient-category cheat sheet from Myth #6 packed into an affordable cream.

We voted this the best drugstore face serum for a reason. It contains Vichy's legendary Volcanic Water, which is sourced from French volcanoes and contains 15 essential minerals that strengthen, protect and repair the skin barrier​.

articles.title: Nepal floods: Over 100 Indians missing; MEA issues helpline numbers
articles.summary: South Asia News: At least 384 travellers, including 105 Indians, have been reported missing following a flash flood in the Bhote Koshi River in Nepalâs Rasuwa district.
articles.body: At least 384 travellers, including 105 Indians, have been reported missing following a flash flood in the Bhote Koshi River in Nepalâs Rasuwa district on Wednesday morning, the Nepal Tourism Board said. The missing travellers include 291 foreign nationals and 93 Nepali nationals.Of the 291 foreign nationals reported missing, others include citizens of Australia, the Netherlands, the United States, Malaysia, the United Kingdom and South Africa.The nationalities of several other foreign travellers are yet to be confirmed, while 37 have been listed as non-resident Indians (NRIs).The Embassy of India in Kathmandu has issued emergency helpline numbers for assistance and information regarding Indian nationals affected by the flash floods in Nepal.Those seeking assistance can contact +977 985 131 6807 or +977 970 910 7500, the MEA said.The preliminary list was compiled using information from 10 tourism and travel agencies. The Tourism Board, Tourist Police and other tourism stakeholders are working with travel agencies, guides, local authorities and security agencies to verify the whereabouts and safety of those reported missing, as cited by Nepal News.The preliminary agency-wise records show that 92 travellers were associated with Trekkers Society, 71 with Samrat Tours & Travels, 55 with Leaf Holiday, 52 with Himalayan Glacier, 31 with Kailash Journey, 27 with Fishtail Tours & Travels, 20 with Alpine Eco Trek, 17 with Kathmandu Holiday Tours & Travels, 12 with Richa Tours & Travels and seven with Explore Vacation.Tourists in the affected areas have been advised to remain calm, stay updated through official channels and follow safety instructions issued by authorities.Those requiring emergency assistance can contact 1234, 1144 or the Tourist Police at 9851289445, Nepal News reported.They can also approach the nearest police or security personnel, local administration, travel agency, guide or tour operator.At least seventeen people have been confirmed dead and more than 25 rescued following the flash flood, Nepal Army officials said, according to local media reports.Police said four bodies were recovered from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot, near the Trishuli River. The Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police have been deployed for search-and-rescue operations, with 14 helicopters, drones and sniffer dogs being used to locate those still missing.The Nepal Army said six people were rescued from Syafrubesi, two from Mailung and four from Dhunche in Rasuwa. It has also established an emergency treatment centre at Military Training Centre No. 1 in Trishuli.Four Armed Police Force personnel were initially reported missing from Rasuwa, while another report said nine personnel stationed at Timure, near the Nepal-China border, remained unaccounted for.A sudden surge in the Bhote Koshi River struck the Rasuwagadhi-Timure area at around 9 am local time, affecting Rasuwa as well as parts of the neighbouring Nuwakot and Dhading districts.The flooding washed away vehicles, goods, bridges and other infrastructure, while several hydropower projects also suffered damage.Amid concerns over a potential flood threat in Bihar following heavy rainfall in Nepal, Union home minister Amit Shah spoke to Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary over the phone, news agency ANI reported.Shah assured the Bihar government of all possible assistance to deal with the situation, while the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is being mobilised to respond to any emergency.Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath also expressed concern over the flood situation in Nepal and directed authorities in vulnerable districts to remain alert.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: California couple confront their surrogate in a Texas court as dispute over newborn escalates
articles.summary: DALLAS — A California couple in an escalating fight with their surrogate over a newborn with a life-threatening heart defect told a Texas court Tuesday that the child’s condition has worsened and they are anguished by attempts to deny them parental rights because they previously wanted an abortion.
articles.body: DALLAS — A California couple in an escalating fight with their surrogate over a newborn with a life-threatening heart defect told a Texas court Tuesday that the child’s condition has worsened and they are anguished by attempts to deny them parental rights because they previously wanted an abortion. “He’s our child,” Nausheen Gilkar said, wiping away tears on the witness stand. “She’s unstable,” Gilkar said of surrogate McKenna West, who was sitting across from her in the Dallas courtroom. “She’s trying to take him from us.” The hearing offered the fullest public airing to date of a deepening and high-profile dispute over surrogacy and abortion that has rushed right-to-life groups and GOP officeholders to the side of West, a nurse who flew from Alaska to have the baby on Aug. 12 in Texas, where most abortions are banned. Gilkar and her husband, Omar Ahmed, say they named the newborn Rumi. Attorneys for West, who has called the child Gabriel, said she is seeking sole conservatorship to make medical decisions for the child. It was not clear when the judge would issue an order in the case. West told the court that she was 23 weeks pregnant when she made an appointment for an abortion at the couple’s urging but was not comfortable with it. “I knew that this baby, despite the diagnosis, had a great chance at survival and a great chance at leading a long life,” West said. After West gave birth, the couple obtained a restraining order barring her from seeing or holding the child. The judge did not rule on final custody or conservatorship Tuesday, and the restraining order was left in effect. Couple say child’s condition has declined ‘significantly’ Court documents filed by the couple’s attorney prior to the hearing said Rumi was in critical condition and appeared to be “suffering from potential complications” from a procedure after he was born. The child has hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a congenital defect in which one side of the organ is underdeveloped, preventing normal blood flow. Fewer than 1,000 newborns each year have the condition, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Without treatment, death can come within days or weeks. Gilkar told the court that the baby had no blood flow to the left side of his heart. Since surgery, she said, he has gasped for air, choked on tubes and needed a blood transfusion. “He’s the most beautiful person I’ve never seen,” Gilkar said. “He’s the love of our lives. He’s suffering a lot.” Surrogate’s attorney presses couple over proposed abortion West and her attorneys have argued that Gilkar and Ahmed were not committed to guaranteeing that the baby would undergo surgeries or “life-saving care.” They say West should have conservatorship because the couple asked her to terminate the pregnancy after learning of the baby’s diagnosis. On the stand, West told their attorney, Lee Budner, that if the court finds that the couple are committed to the baby receiving the surgeries, she would drop any custody claims. Jeff Domen, an attorney for West, repeatedly pressed Gilkar on the couple’s desire to terminate the pregnancy, asking her to confirm that she requested it. Asked if she regretted the decision, Gilkar responded that she did not. “Would you trust somebody to care for your child that wanted your child dead?” Domen asked. Gilkar said she did not know how to respond to the question. Accusations that surrogate broke contract Gilkar and Ahmed say West violated the surrogacy contract they entered in August 2025. Gilkar told the court that she entered the contract after going through eight rounds of in vitro fertilization in Los Angeles and her body “gave up.” She had to undergo a hysterectomy, she said. “It was not my first choice, it was my only option,” Gilkar said. West stayed in the couple’s home in Los Angeles, Gilkar said, and she was there with West for the IVF transfer. “I was holding her hand,” Gilkar said, crying. The couple’s attorney referenced court records from California that determined West has no rights to legal or physical custody. West said she wanted the judge to disregard that ruling, saying she was willing to fight for him since the diagnosis. Surrogacy is not regulated on a federal level, and experts say each state has its own laws, which can leave room for gaps in interpretation. “We believe Ms. West is the mother of this child,” Domen said.

articles.title: Hundreds missing as flash flood sweeps villages near Nepal-Tibet border
articles.summary: Three Americans are among hundreds of people missing after torrential floods swept through the Himalayan border areas of Nepal and China’s Tibet.
articles.body: A wall of mud and rock appeared to collapse ​into a river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and China’s Tibet on Wednesday, triggering catastrophic flooding on the Nepali side that killed at least 31 people and left ‌hundreds of tourists missing. In a still-unfolding disaster, verified videos showed dozens of people swept away at the border, with authorities on both sides fearing far higher casualties and massive destruction. Houses, roads and power projects were swept away in Nepal, while officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” with some missing in the county of Gyirong after a mudslide hit a border land crossing. Initial reports suggested that an earthquake in the area could have triggered an avalanche and caused the floods, ​Nepal’s foreign minister Shisir Khanal told the country’s parliament on Wednesday, local media reported. At least 384 travellers, including 105 Indians, 93 Nepalis, three U.S. citizens and 12 British nationals were missing ​from the region, Nepal’s tourism authority said. South Korean news agency Yonhap separately reported that about eight of its nationals were also unaccounted for in Nepal. Flood ⁠alerts were issued in the populous northern Indian states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar as they border Nepal and several rivers flow down the mountains into their plains. Experts fear a second flood Security footage captured ​on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border showed many people fleeing before a wall of rock, mud and water destroyed buildings, vehicles and took many lives. The exact cause of the mudslide could not be ​immediately determined, but the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) said there was a 4.4 magnitude quake approximately seven minutes before the time shown on the security footage time-stamp. An ice-rock avalanche in the Lhende Khola river on the Nepali side was the trigger, but the cause remains unconfirmed, said Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks, at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development. “With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood ​may occur,” Qianggong said. Rescue helicopters could not land in Nepal’s affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa, with a population of about 50,000, officials said, with the river flowing above its normal course. Television broadcast images of crumbled homes in the floodwaters, floating cars and a metal bridge being washed away, while witnesses told Reuters the waters engulfed entire villages. “There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” said district administrator Narendra Pariyar, who urged dwellers on the banks of the Bhote Koshi river to move to higher ground, after reports of villages and project sites being swept up. “There is devastation everywhere we look,” Tula Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa, told Reuters. “The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing.” Nepal’s rescue helicopters would be unable to land in the affected areas until the waters recede, army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said. The cause of the inundation was not immediately clear, but a deadly flash flood on the same river last year was eventually traced to the draining of a glacier lake. China’s official Xinhua news agency said the mudslide occurred on the Nepali side and hit the Gyirong port to cut roads, communications and power links in the Shigatse region near the border with Nepal, but did not elaborate. President Xi Jinping urged “all-out” search efforts for the missing as well as stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters. Nepal’s energy ministry said 430 MW of electricity supplies were affected, mostly from hydroelectric projects, or more than 12% of total national hydropower capacity of 3.2 GW, a Reuters calculation showed. Police and military were joining in the rescue effort, said Prime Minister Balendra Shah. “Instructions have been given ... to move the people living in the lower areas to safer places,” he said. “People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert.” From its origins in Tibet, the Bhote Koshi river empties into Nepal’s Trishuli river that eventually flows into India as the Gandak river. Last year’s Bhote Koshi flood killed nine people, with 24 missing, as it washed away a “Friendship Bridge” linking Nepal and China to disrupt trade and transport for months. That flood was triggered by the draining of a supraglacial lake in Tibet, a regional climate monitor said.

articles.title: Photos: Thousands join Spain’s La Tomatina festival for epic tomato battle
articles.summary: About 20,000 participants hurled 165 tonnes of tomatoes in Bunol’s streets during Spain’s famed La Tomatina festival.
articles.body:
Thousands of revellers have packed into the narrow streets of Buñol in eastern Spain for La Tomatina, the town’s annual tomato-throwing festival that has become one of the country’s most distinctive summer attractions.

For about an hour on Wednesday, trucks unloaded up to 165 tonnes of overripe tomatoes into the crowd as festival-goers, many in white T-shirts, hurled the fruit at each other to a soundtrack of blasting pop music.

Authorities covered buildings with tarps before the melee and deployed police, who at one point appeared to use pepper spray to disperse part of the crowd before the festivities quickly resumed.

More than 20,000 people were expected to attend, with Spanish media reporting that about 40 percent of participants in recent years are international tourists, including a growing number from India following the 2011 Bollywood film Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara.

La Tomatina, held on the last Wednesday of August, began with a local food fight in 1945 and survived a ban under Francisco Franco before television turned it into a global spectacle.
