articles.title: Tom Byabagamba: Ex-head of Rwandan President Paul Kagame's presidential guard dies in jail 12 years after his arrest
articles.summary: His brother tells the BBC his family have not been allowed to see him "in all these years".
articles.body:
Former head of Rwanda's presidential guard Tom Byabagamba, 59, who once served as President Paul Kagame's personal bodyguard, has died in jail.

He was arrested in 2014 along with his brother-in-law Frank Rusagara, a retired brigadier-general, for "spreading rumours" and "tarnishing the image of the country and government".

Right groups expressed concern over their cases, framing them as a part of a pattern of government repression. Throughout his trial, Col Byabagamba denied the allegations against him, saying they were fabricated.

Byabagamba's brother David Himbara told the BBC Great Lakes service his family did not know the cause of death as "no-one was allowed to see him in all these years".

Rights groups have repeatedly accused Kagame's government of restricting political opposition and silencing critics within Rwanda and abroad.

In 2016, a military court convicted Byagamba and imprisoned him for 21 years, although this was later reduced to 15 years on appeal. Rusagara, who had also been secretary-general of the defence ministry, was given a 20-year sentence.

Rusagara died in prison in March last year. At the time Human Rights Watch (HRW) described it as the "lonely death of a general", noting that his family had not heard his voice since 2014, days before his arrest.

His family was informed by the authorities that Rusagara had been ill with cancer, the rights group said.

The conviction of the two men had followed a "flawed trial" marked by "serious allegations of torture and witness tampering", according to HRW.

Campaign group Freedom Now had also previously criticised their detention as "arbitrary" and as having "violated international law".

Byabagamba leaves behind two sons and a wife.

articles.title: Delhi court convicts Sukesh Chandrasekhar for posing as SC judge to seek bail
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court has convicted alleged conman Sukesh Chandrasekhar for impersonating a sitting Supreme Court judge to influence a special judg.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court has convicted alleged conman Sukesh Chandrasekhar for impersonating a sitting Supreme Court judge to influence a special judge into granting him bail in a 2017 corruption case.The court described the act as a "direct affront" to the independence and sanctity of the judicial process, news agency PTI reported.Chief judicial magistrate Harshita Mishra held Chandrasekhar guilty under IPC Sections 170 (personating a public servant), 189 (threat of injury to a public servant) and 507 (criminal intimidation by an anonymous communication).The court will hear arguments on the quantum of sentence on August 27.In an order dated August 20, the court said, "The present case shall for posterity remain a reminder that the majesty of law does not reside in the voice of an individual, however authoritative it may sound over a telephone, but in the integrity of the judicial process itself."The case relates to a phone call made on April 28, 2017, when Chandrasekhar was in police custody in connection with the corruption case.According to the prosecution, he gained access to the mobile phone of police constable Manjeet and used it to contact the official landline and mobile phone of Poonam Chaudhary, then special judge handling Prevention of Corruption Act cases.The court said Chandrasekhar initially impersonated the private secretary of a then sitting Supreme Court judge and later impersonated the judge himself.He allegedly sought to persuade Chaudhary to grant him bail at the earliest and threatened her with adverse professional consequences if she did not comply, PTI reported."A courtroom may be entered through its doors, but justice cannot be entered through the backdoor of impersonation, intimidation or manufactured authority. The accused attempted precisely such a backdoor entry into the judicial process. The evidence has closed that door," the court said.The judge said the case was qualitatively different from an ordinary cheating or impersonation matter as the alleged conduct sought to undermine judicial independence by invoking the authority of the country's highest court to influence another judicial officer."The court also finds it necessary to record that the conduct of the accused constitutes a direct affront to the independence and sanctity of the judicial process. Courts decide cases on the basis of law and evidence, not on the basis of telephone calls purporting to emanate from persons occupying positions of authority," the judge said.The court said the prosecution had established beyond reasonable doubt that Chandrasekhar deliberately assumed the identity of a Supreme Court judge to interfere with the administration of justice."The accused sought to use that borrowed authority not for any legitimate purpose, but to procure a judicial outcome favourable to himself. The brazenness of the attempt cannot dilute the offence; rather, it demonstrates the deliberateness with which the criminal design was executed," the judge said.It held that the impersonation was not incidental but "the very instrument" used to achieve his unlawful objective, as he understood that the words of a Supreme Court judge would carry an authority his own identity could not command.The court also found the ingredients of IPC Section 189 (threat of injury to public servant) made out, saying Chandrasekhar attempted to induce a judicial officer to exercise her discretion in a particular manner by invoking the supposed authority of a superior constitutional court.It further held that the anonymous nature of the communication attracted IPC Section 507 (criminal intimidation by an anonymous communication), PTI reported.Calling the conduct a direct affront to the judicial process, the court said allowing such attempts to be treated as mere deception could embolden people to circumvent courtrooms by manufacturing authority outside them."The judicial process cannot be allowed to become vulnerable to such manufactured commands," it said.The court, however, also directed Delhi Police to re-examine the role of constable Manjeet, including how Chandrasekhar obtained access to his mobile phone, whether it was locked, who knew its password and why the alleged use of the phone was not promptly reported.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: CIA chief held talks with Russian intelligence services, Kremlin says
articles.summary: John Ratcliffe travelled to the Russian capital on Tuesday in a rare and unannounced visit.
articles.body:
The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) met figures from Russia's intelligence services during his unannounced visit to Moscow on Tuesday, the Kremlin has confirmed.

John Ratcliffe travelled to the Russian capital on Tuesday but neither side has shed any light on what prompted the unconventional meeting or what was discussed.

It is rare for American senior intelligence leaders to travel to Russia, with the last comparable meeting taking place in the months leading up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow on board a military plane which left later the same day.

The Kremlin ruled out speculation the CIA head met Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"There were contacts with the intelligence services," Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

"There were no meetings with the president of Russia. That's all I can say on the subject. Naturally, President Putin is briefed immediately about everything," he added.

Peskov made the comments in response to a question at his daily press briefing from a reporter at the Russian newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta, who asked if Vladimir Putin was informed about the CIA chief meetings and "at what level" they were held.

Putin's spokesman was also asked by the BBC's Russia Editor Steve Rosenberg what was the topic of the CIA talks.

"I have nothing to add to what I've already said on the subject," Peskov replied.

It was too early to say what impact this meeting would have over repairing bilateral US-Russian relations, he said, telling reporters: "How much this will impact the overall process of recovering our bilateral relations from the profound crisis they're currently in, it is premature to say."

But contacts between intelligence agencies are "a positive phenomenon, a positive process," Peskov added, saying they often continue "even during the most difficult moments" in relations between the two countries.

Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.

There has been no official comment on Ratcliffe's visitfrom the CIA, White House or Pentagon.

Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit Russia during President Donald Trump's second term.

The last time a CIA director visited Moscow was in November 2021, when William Burns warned Russia against sending troops into Ukraine. Weeks later, the Kremlin launched its full-scale war on Ukraine.

Since then, the US has had strained relations with Russia, which has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.

Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.

John Foreman, who served as a British military attaché to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."

articles.title: In 1967, Emily Frew Oliver sold her familyâs Wyoming dude ranch to Grand Teton National Park but kept a life estate; 39 years later she gave it up, ending her familyâs 79-year stewardship of the historic ranch
articles.summary: US News: The 4 Lazy F Ranch sits on the west bank of the Snake River in Wyoming, just north of the Grand Teton National Park headquarters in Moose. Below the T.
articles.body: The 4 Lazy F Ranch sits on the west bank of the Snake River in Wyoming, just north of the Grand Teton National Park headquarters in Moose. Below the Teton Range, the ranch preserves a part of the areaâs homestead and dude ranch history.The property was first known as the Sun Star Ranch. Bryant Mears filed a claim for a 160-acre homestead in 1914 after arriving in Jackson Hole as a dude at the Bar BC Ranch, according to History Jackson Hole. He later served in the US Army during the First World War before returning to the valley with his wife.Mears received his homestead patent in 1921, but he had already transferred the property to Edward Mears. Edward later sold it to William and Margaretta Frew in 1927. The family renamed it the 4 Lazy F Ranch, a name based on the 'four Frews'- William, Margaretta and their two daughters, Margaretta 'Peggy' and Emily.For the Frews, the property initially served as a summer retreat. They built the main lodge and sleeping cabins, along with other structures that helped shape the ranch. The layout followed a style associated with Rocky Mountain dude ranches, with the main lodge at the centre and sleeping cabins arranged around it.From family retreat to dude ranchThe Frew family made few additions to the property between 1927 and 1949. That changed after William Frew died in 1948 and Margaretta Frew died in 1949. Emily Frew Oliver inherited the ranch and decided to open it to paying guests in 1950.Emily and her husband, Henry Oliver Jr, ran the ranch together. Henry looked after outdoor activities, including pack and fishing trips, while Emily managed the cooking and cleaning staff. She also made sure meals were prepared for both guests and staff.The ranch offered a different type of stay from many dude ranches in the valley. While a typical dude ranch stay was around two weeks, the 4 Lazy F accepted visitors for anything from an overnight stay to several weeks. A Union Pacific Railroad guide from around 1960 advertised rooms with meals, riding, swimming, fishing and pack trips to Yellowstone National Park.The ranch continued to retain much of its earlier character even as it operated for guests. Its main lodge served as the living and dining area, with a large central living room and fireplace. Sleeping cabins surrounded the lodge and created a communal area for guests. Irrigation ditches built during the earlier ranching period remained on the property, although they are no longer used.Property largely unchangedThe Olivers also continued the ranchâs agricultural activities. They kept milk cows, work horses, saddle horses, hogs and chickens. The family cultivated and irrigated land for winter feed but made few other changes to the landscape.The propertyâs natural appearance was part of its character. The lawn outside the main lodge was one of the main areas that was altered. It was first irrigated and flooded to keep the grass green, before the Olivers later installed a sprinkler system.As the ranch developed, some new buildings were added. A sleeping cabin and casting pond were constructed in 1952. Another cabin was moved from the Circle H Ranch in 1954, while the River Cabin was moved to the property in 1961. In 1964, a new cabin was built and parts of the caretakerâs cabin were modified.The ranch remained closely tied to the Oliver family. After Henry Oliver Jr died in 1977, their oldest son, Harry, helped Emily maintain and run the property. From 1977 to 2005, he spent every May through October at the ranch, overseeing operations and general maintenance.The 1967 sale to National ParkIn 1967, Emily Frew Oliver sold the 4 Lazy F Ranch to the federal government. However, she reserved a life estate, allowing her to retain her rights to the property during her lifetime.The sale marked a major change in ownership, but it did not immediately end the familyâs connection with the ranch. The Olivers continued to use and maintain the property for decades. The ranch formally stopped accepting paying guests during the 1990s.Emily Oliver eventually decided to voluntarily terminate her life estate. In 2006, she gave up the remaining rights and turned over management of the 4 Lazy F Ranch to the National Park Service.Today, the 4 Lazy F Ranch is vacant while the National Park Service evaluates possible future uses for the property. Its historic buildings remain, including the lodge, sleeping cabins, caretakerâs cabin, barn and other outbuildings.Several landscape features also survive. The lawn and ornamental plantings can still be seen, while native vegetation remains around the lodge and caretakerâs house. articles.title: In 2018, Florida opened Americaâs first permanent underwater sculpture garden 58 feet below the Gulf; it has grown into a living reef where more than 100 species have been documented
articles.summary: US News: Imagine you are diving under the Gulf of Mexico and come upon what looks like a museum, only instead of galleries and polished floors, there is an unr.
articles.body: Imagine you are diving under the Gulf of Mexico and come upon what looks like a museum, only instead of galleries and polished floors, there is an unreal world of sculptures, tropical fish and drifting sea life. Florida's Underwater Museum of Art has turned the ocean floor into a gallery at 58 feet below the surface, where art is slowly becoming part of nature. Located about 0.93 miles off the shore of Grayton Beach State Park in Walton County, the Underwater Museum of Art (UMA) is the first permanent underwater sculpture garden in the United States. But it is more than an unusual destination for divers. Its sculptures have been designed specifically to be artificial reefs, creating habitat on an area dominated by barren sand. Scroll down to read the details.Art Meets the GulfAccording to its official website, the museum was a collaboration between the Cultural Arts Alliance of Walton County and the South Walton Artificial Reef Association in 2018. The idea was simple, but ambitious: merge artistic expression with marine conservation. Artists from around the country and the world are invited to submit sculptures for consideration each year. Selected works are engineered, transported and carefully positioned on the sea bed. They are built to endure a harsh environment and to support marine life, not conventional museum pieces. Artists and organizers must meet certain requirements for materials, structural integrity and ecological safety, including requirements that allow sea turtles to escape safely if they become trapped. The result is an ever-changing underwater gallery.A museum that turns into a reefThe sculptures are not just objects that are submerged in water. They become living structures in time. Here, artificial reefs offer surfaces and shelter for fish, invertebrates and other marine organisms. The structures can offer cover and breeding habitat for small creatures, and the baitfish attract larger predators. Juvenile fish can also take shelter as they grow. That ecological role is especially vital in Walton County, where much of the Gulfâs coastal seafloor is open sand flats.Since the museum opened, more than 100 species of marine and plant life have been recorded around the sculptures. Dolphins and sea turtles, along with a range of fish and invertebrates, are also found. For scientists, the site offers more than a beautiful underwater landscape. It offers an opportunity to monitor the development of artificial reef systems and their potential impacts on marine environments.A gallery of odd and wonderful artThe sculptures vary from playful to monumental. One of them is âPoseidonâs Throneâ, which is at once a symbolic seat of power and habitat for marine organisms. âA Common Chordâ takes the form of a giant guitar, and celebrates the relationship between humans and nature. Other installations are âThree Wishes,â a genie lamp that divers can play with by blowing air into small openings, and âI Found It,â a giant diamond ring lying on the Gulf floor. A giant octopus, a skull, a seashell and a pirate shipwreck augment the otherworldly atmosphere. The works together form a landscape that is part art exhibition and part sunken fantasy and part thriving ecosystem.A laboratory of life below the seaUMA has drawn in divers and art lovers, as well as marine scientists, ecologists, wildlife professionals and students. Researchers can observe artificial structures transform into working habitats as the sculptures slowly get colonized by marine organisms. It is therefore both an ecotourism attraction and an ongoing experiment in the conservation of the marine environment. The project has also garnered international attention, being featured by major media outlets and recognized as a notable travel destination.Exploring the underwater museumThe museum is free for scuba divers but you need proper diving experience to get there. Visitors must be qualified divers and comfortable with open sea conditions. Dive excursions range from the coast near Grayton Beach State Park to the submerged site, where visitors can explore the sculptures and the marine life that has made them home. What started as a curious collaboration between artists and conservationists in 2018 has morphed into something much more interesting: a museum that changes every year. Its sculptures may have been carved by humans but down under the Gulf, nature is also dabbling in art.Images Courtesy: Underwater Museum of ArtCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Heart, hope and a steely determination: Dolly Parton's musical legacy
articles.summary: BBC music correspondent Mark Savage looks back on the legacy of the "irreplaceable" late singer.
articles.body:
But her guitar was banned from the set - so she made the beat by strumming her acrylic nails together.

The sound, she realised, was just like the typewriter used by her character, a married secretary who is constantly belittled and sexually harassed by her boss.

Excited, she ran over and sang the song to her co-stars Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, who was also the film's producer.

"Lily and I looked at each other and we had goosebumps," Fonda said. "And we knew, this is not just a movie song, this is an anthem."

Taylor Swift and Beyoncé lead tributes after death of 'bold and brilliant' Dolly Parton

How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs

'If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain': The wit and wisdom of Dolly Parton

Released in November 1980, 9 To 5 became Parton's only US number one as a solo artist, and earned her an Oscar nomination for best song.

She loved to tell the fingernail story, but 9 To 5 has another legacy - for its powerful statements about working life and women's place in the corporate world.

You can probably sing the hook off the top of your head. " Working 9 To 5 / What a way to make a living! " It's jaunty and catchy. The sentiment is universal. Work sucks.

But dig deeper and Dolly's expressing real fury.

" It's a rich man's game, no matter what they call it / And you spend your life putting money in his wallet ," she sings. " They just use your mind and they never give you credit. "

The lyrics tapped into real frustrations and gave working women a voice.

But there's a reason why you might not have noticed the anger that fuels Dolly's song. She simply doesn't sing it that way - even though she had every right to, having navigated the sexism of the music industry from the age of 13.

Her early breakthrough came in 1967 when she was hired as the "girl singer" on The Porter Wagoner Show, a TV showcase for country singer Porter Wagoner that reached millions of viewers each week.

Together, they released 21 hit duets including Just Someone I Used to Know, If Teardrops Were Pennies and Please Don't Stop Loving Me.

But as Parton's star rose, she began to outshine her co-star. Eventually, she realised she needed to strike out as a solo artist – writing I Will Always Love You as a letter of apology to her former mentor. He responded by suing her for breach of contract in 1979, demanding $3m (£2,2m).

Wanting to avoid a lengthy court battle, Parton settled for about $1m.

"I made up my mind that if he could live with it, I could live without it," she wrote in her autobiography. "I suppose Porter has done all right with it. I am neither his conscience nor his accountant."

It was typical of the star's ability to radiate cheery goodwill that she never held a grudge against Wagoner, always crediting him with giving her a crucial career break, even after their relationship fell apart.

But she was nobody's fool. Take, for example, the battle over the rights to I Will Always Love You.

After it hit number one in the country charts, Elvis Presley called – he loved the song and wanted to record a cover.

"You cannot imagine how excited I am about this," she told him. "This is the greatest thing that's ever happened to me as a songwriter."

But the night before the recording session, his notoriously hard-nosed manager, Colonel Tom Parker, called Parton and told her Elvis wouldn't record the song unless she handed over half of the lucrative publishing rights.

"I said, 'Well, that throws a new light on this. Because I can't give you half the publishing. I'm gonna leave that to my family,'" Parton told Reba McEntire's podcast in 2020.

"And he said, 'Well, then we can't do it.' And I cried all night."

"I mean, it was like the worst thing," she told Country Music Television. "People were saying, 'You're nuts. It's Elvis Presley. Hell, I'd give him all of it.'

"I said, 'I can't.' I always wondered what it would sound like. I know he would have killed it [in a good way]."

When Whitney Houston recorded her blockbuster version of I Will Always Love You for The Bodyguard soundtrack in 1992, the country star still owned the rights and earned "enough money to buy Graceland", Presley's mansion.

Instead, she invested the money in a black neighbourhood in Nashville, Tennessee, saying she thought it was an apt way to honour Houston's legacy.

That determination to stand up for herself, and to value her music as more than just a commodity, is an essential part of Parton's legacy.

Without her example, would Taylor Swift have stood up to the hedge funds who bought her back catalogue, re-recording her biggest hits to rob them of royalties?

Perhaps not – but either way, Dolly approved.

"Smart!" she said when asked about Swift's masterplan. "She's so smart, she's so great, she's genius. I mean really, look at what she's doing! That's amazing!"

Mourning Parton's death, Swift acknowledged the star's "backbone of steel" in the struggle "to defend her own self worth as an artist".

Musically, her legacy is just as profound.

Parton was about six years old when she wrote her first song: Little Tiny Tasseltop, an ode to her favourite doll and its corn-silk hair.

For the rest of her career, she turned everyday details like those into songs of hope and heart.

Her 1971 classic Coat of Many Colors tells the profoundly moving story of Parton as a child being proud of the ragged, hand-sewn clothes her mother had made for her.

The 1974 concept album My Tennessee Mountain Home, meanwhile, is a musical autobiography that opens with Parton reciting the first letter she wrote home after moving to Nashville as a teenager.

" A couple of folks already told me that they might record a couple of my songs, so I'll be makin' enough money to get by ," she sang. " And I don't want you to be worrying about me bein' hungry or anything ."

The album cover is a photo of the two-room log cabin that was Parton's actual childhood home in the 1940s and 50s, and the rest of the songs paint an idyllic picture of her childhood.

Even when the family didn't have electricity and running water, she was determined to see the good in everyone and every situation.

" We might have been poor but we didn't know it / We'd heard that word but we didn't know what it meant. "

Her diaristic approach to songwriting also gave birth to hits like Jolene – written about a red-headed love rival – and All I Can Do, a heartfelt declaration of love to her husband, Carl Dean.

Funny and authentic, she captured the trials and tribulations of life in a way that was always relatable, even when her stage outfits and her hairstyle remained larger than life.

The feminist message of 9 To 5 was preceded by When Possession Gets Too Strong and Just Because I'm A Woman, which castigated double standards in relationships: " My mistakes are no worse than yours / Just because I'm a woman ."

And in an era where women were forced into gendered stereotypes – housewife, temptress, fallen woman, mixed-up girl – she satirised and sent up those roles, playing them to the hilt while emphasising her strength.

" I've always been misunderstood because of how I look ," she sang on 2008's Backwood Barbie. " Don't judge me by the cover, cos I'm a real good book ."

Words like those inspired generations of women to be who they were, not who the world perceived them as.

And she used her music to unite people, even as much of the country music establishment entrenched itself in conservatism.

In 2002, at the House of Blues in Los Angeles, Parton even replaced the name Jolene with "drag queen" as a crowd of drag performers looked on.

Outside music, her philanthropy gave scholarships to impoverished students and supplied more than 200 million books to young readers.

Significantly, none of the country stars she inspired were ever billed as "the next Dolly Parton" because no-one did it like Dolly. She was unique. Irreplaceable. Unreproducible.

A legend in her lifetime, and now beyond.

Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millions

Dolly Parton was the one thing most Americans could agree on

articles.title: Why India is sharing missile secrets with its private sector
articles.summary: New policy allows India’s private sector to produce advanced weaponry, supporting its goal of military self-sufficiency.
articles.body:
India has taken a major step towards opening one of its most sensitive areas of defence production to private companies.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh approved the transfer of technologies developed by the state-run Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) for all conventional missile systems to Indian industry for domestic production, the country’s Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday.

The move marks a significant shift for the sector dominated by government-run firms and research laboratories. Private companies will be able to compete for the technology and production rights, subject to technical qualifications, certifications and other regulatory requirements, the ministry said.

The Narendra Modi-led government says the aim is to move missiles from development into mass production faster, increase domestic manufacturing and reduce India’s dependence on imports.

So, does India’s private defence industry have the capacity to manufacture sophisticated missile systems at the scale and reliability the military needs, is the country moving towards developing its own military-industrial complex, and are there security risks involved?

India’s Defence Ministry said Singh had approved the transfer of DRDO-developed technology for all conventional missile systems to Indian defence companies for production inside the country.

“The objective is to enhance domestic manufacturing capabilities, strengthen the defence industrial base, and create opportunities for the participation of Indian MSMEs (micro, small and medium-sized enterprises) and other technology partners in the supply chain,” the ministry said in a statement.

The measure would enable the “successful transition of missile system development to industrial production” and create opportunities for MSMEs and other technology partners, the ministry added.

“DRDO remains committed to working closely with Indian industry to facilitate the transfer and absorption of advanced defence technologies and to further strengthen the country’s indigenous defence capabilities.”

The announcement spans a wide range of missiles, said Aditya Ramanathan, a research fellow with the Bengaluru-based Takshashila Institution.

“It will include surface-to-air missiles, air-to-air missiles, anti-radiation missiles, antitank systems, and so on. It will also include more heavy-duty hardware like land-attack cruise missiles,” he told Al Jazeera.

India has traditionally relied heavily on state-owned defence companies to turn weapons developed by DRDO into large-scale production. Bharat Dynamics, one such state-owned company, has long held a monopoly in missile production.

Tuesday’s announcement is a “big change” because it ends that monopoly, said Ramanathan.

“Private companies have been making missile components for years, but what this decision does is allow them to move up the value chain and become prime integrators for these systems,” he said.

While India largely relies on domestically made missiles, it also imports missiles — especially from Russia and Israel, two key weapons suppliers to the country.

But under Modi, India has attempted to both encourage self-reliance in defence — a concept that the government calls Atmanirbhar Bharat or self-reliant India — and prod foreign defence majors to manufacture in India.

At a time when geopolitical allegiances are changing fast, and India faces uncertainties on both major borders — with rivals Pakistan and China — the country under Modi has more than doubled its defence budget, from $38bn in 2014 to $86bn in the current financial year.

The brief four-day conflict with nuclear-armed rival and neighbour Pakistan last year has injected fresh urgency into India’s defence preparedness plans. This year’s defence budget is 16 percent higher than the previous year’s.

Other geopolitical events have forced the government’s hand too, suggested Ramanathan.

“I don’t think this move would have happened as soon as it did if not for the experience of recent wars. Indian decision-makers have been looking at Ukraine, they’ve been looking at the US war with Iran, and of course they’ve been imbibing the lessons of operations from last year,” he said.

“One reason you’re going to need large stockpiles is that, as we’ve seen recently, you’re going to burn through your inventory pretty quickly. The other reason is that your adversary could also degrade your stockpiles using their own precision-strike systems.”

China, he said, was a major factor in India’s calculations.

“India believes that to deter China, which is its most capable adversary, it will need to demonstrate that it can both inflict and absorb really punishing attrition over weeks of gruelling warfare,” Ramanathan said.

To that end, India is also creating a tri-services conventional missile force. “To be a viable and effective force, it’s going to require serious magazine depth, and this cannot be achieved without the active involvement of the private sector,” he added.

What is India’s defence industry already manufacturing?

In June, India announced that it was preparing to spend more than $2bn on military drones from domestic manufacturers, reflecting the rapid expansion of the country’s private defence industry.

More than 600 companies were involved in India’s drone industry, including major groups such as Adani, Larsen & Toubro, and Tata Advanced Systems, as well as startups.

In July, India also approved the purchase of a range of military equipment for its defence forces worth $5.46bn, including missiles, electronic warfare systems and Kamikaze drones.

India is also pushing to rapidly modernise its navy with an eye on Beijing’s growing influence in key Indian Ocean shipping lanes. In December, New Delhi announced plans to procure at least 75 ships and submarines, with most expected to be constructed domestically.

At the same time, India is trying to diversify the foreign sources of its weapons. Over the past decade, New Delhi has worked to move away from its longstanding reliance on Russia for military hardware, expanding defence ties with countries such as the United States, France and — increasingly — Israel.

Does the private sector have the capacity to build missiles?

Private arms manufacturers in India have been increasing spending on bolstering military production in the past few years.

Major conglomerates have invested heavily in ammunition, drones, aerospace and military electronics. Of late, they have started to invest in facilities that aim to manufacture missiles.

Adani Defence & Aerospace, owned by business tycoon Gautam Adani, a close associate of Indian Prime Minister Modi, announced plans in 2024 to invest more than 30 billion rupees ($315m) in ammunition and missile manufacturing facilities in Uttar Pradesh.

The facilities would include capabilities for handling explosives used in missiles and precision munitions.

But commitments and intent don’t build missiles.

“Ultimately, I think the success or failure of this move will depend on how the Indian government places orders,” Ramanathan said. “Making missiles is an incredibly complex and costly affair, and companies are going to have to invest a lot in infrastructure, technology and people. These sorts of investments will only pay off if the government places large enough orders to justify them and also, hopefully, leave these companies with some profits that they can pour back into research and development.”

India has a range of cruise and ballistic missiles, several of which are also capable of carrying nuclear warheads.

In May, on the anniversary of the 2025 war with Pakistan, India successfully test-fired the Agni-V, its most advanced nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile that can reach a distance of 5,500km (3,418 miles) — a range that covers all of China, the Middle East and even parts of Europe.

Its other ballistic missiles have ranges from as little as the Prithvi-1 (150km or 93 miles) to the Agni-IV (4,000km or 2,485 miles), again covering everything from border skirmishes with Pakistan to India’s extended neighbourhood.

It also has powerful cruise missiles, like the BrahMos, co-developed with Russia, which has a range of up to 500km (311 miles), and was used in last year’s war with Pakistan.

Is India also exporting missiles and other weapons?

India has dramatically ramped up its military exports in recent years, from just $72m in 2014-15 — when Modi came to power — to $4bn in 2025-2016.

Paras Defence, one of India’s fast-growing defence manufacturers, said this month it expects its exports to more than double in the 2026–27 financial year, up to $14m, driven partly by increased demand linked to conflicts in the Middle East.

Indian arms makers have also been involved in joint ventures with companies abroad. Adani Defence, in partnership with Elbit Systems – Israel’s largest weapons manufacturer – produces the large Hermes 900 armed drone systems.

A 2024 investigation by Al Jazeera exposed how India was exporting rocket parts and ammunition to Israel, even as the Modi government was publicly calling for diplomacy to end the war on Gaza.

In June 2026, Amnesty International said in a report that India’s weapons exports to Israel made it complicit in the genocide in Gaza.

But it isn’t just Israel that has sought and received weapons from Indian manufacturers. Nor is it just bullets and weapons parts that India is exporting today — complete missiles are in demand, too.

In 2022, the Philippines bought three batteries of the BrahMos missiles from India. Since then, Vietnam and Indonesia have signed deals with India for the purchase of these missiles. And India has submitted a proposal to the United Arab Emirates offering to supply the Gulf country these missiles, too.

Is the latest move a step towards building a military-industrial complex?

While Tuesday’s announcement marks the first time that India’s state-run research and manufacturing facilities will transfer missile technology to the private sector, the government earlier this year shortlisted private firms to manufacture the country’s next-generation fighter jets.

Tata Advanced Systems, a subsidiary of Tata Sons, and Bharat Forge are among companies to be shortlisted, and are emerging as major makers of artillery systems, ammunition and aerospace systems. India has its homegrown jets, but imports the most cutting-edge planes in its arsenal, including the Rafale fighters from France. The Indian Air Force also relies heavily on Soviet-era jets.

Still, while India “wants to build a wider defence industrial base”, said Ramanathan, “it is very far from developing the sort of military-industrial complex that [former US President Dwight] Eisenhower worried about. Power in India still resides overwhelmingly with the government.”

Despite the surge in domestic manufacturing and exports of specific weapons systems and parts, India on the whole remains a major military importer.

India was the world’s second-largest importer of weapons between 2021 and 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI): Russia was its biggest source, accounting for 40 percent of India’s imported weapons.

Are there risks in transferring sensitive technology to the private sector?

As the US and Israel bombed Iran in March this year, a group of Iranian hackers claimed it broke into the servers of major US defence manufacturer Lockheed Martin, stealing blueprints of components used in the F-35 fighter jets.

The alleged data breach exposed the risks of private companies — which often have lower security standards and oversight than top-secret government laboratories — holding sensitive information.

But Ramanathan pointed out that in India’s case, “the companies that are most likely to get the missile contracts are all old hands”.

“They’ve been involved in the defence sector in some capacity for decades, and they have experience in dealing with confidentiality and secrecy,” he said.

The Indian government, on its part, also “doesn’t want the technology or its missile secrets to go to its adversaries, and it also wants to abide by its commitments to the Missile Technology Control Regime, which gives India several advantages,” he said, referring to one of the world’s major export-control regimes.

“So India has good reasons, in its own self-interest, to ensure that missile technology doesn’t leak.”

articles.title: New York City restaurants are saving 800 pounds of oyster shells from landfills every day and sending them to rebuild reefs, with 19 acres of reef habitat already restored
articles.summary: US News: New York City restaurants are giving discarded oyster shells a second life by keeping hundreds of pounds of them out of landfills every day and sendin.
articles.body: New York City restaurants are giving discarded oyster shells a second life by keeping hundreds of pounds of them out of landfills every day and sending them to a project rebuilding oyster reefs across New York Harbor. The Billion Oyster Project collects more than 300,000 pounds of shells from participating restaurants each year, equivalent to roughly 800 pounds a day. Instead of becoming waste, the shells are cleaned, cured and eventually used as a foundation for new oyster reefs. The effort is part of a much larger restoration programme that has already helped return more than 200 million oysters to New York Harbor and restore about 19 acres of reef habitat. The unusual recycling effort is turning a common restaurant waste product into material for rebuilding a lost marine ecosystem.New York City restaurants are saving hundreds of pounds of oyster shellsThe shell collection programme has created a direct link between New York Cityâs restaurants and the restoration of its harbour. Participating seafood restaurants and oyster bars separate used shells from their normal waste, allowing them to be collected and transported for restoration instead of being sent to landfill. The Billion Oyster Project says its restaurant network sends more than 300,000 pounds of oyster shells to the programme each year. That works out at approximately 800 pounds every day. The shells are particularly valuable because they can provide the hard surface young oysters need when they settle and grow. What begins as waste on a restaurant plate can therefore become part of the physical structure of a new underwater reef.The shells are cured before returning to the harbourThe discarded shells cannot simply be taken from a restaurant and placed directly into the water. They first undergo a lengthy curing process designed to remove remaining organic material and reduce the risk of introducing harmful organisms into the harbour. The Billion Oyster Project processes the shells on Governors Island, where they are cleaned and left to cure for months. The curing period can last close to a year, allowing the shells to become suitable for restoration work. Once they have been prepared, they can be incorporated into reef structures and used as substrate for young oysters. This careful process transforms what would have been food waste into a safe and useful material for marine restoration.The shells become the foundation for new oyster reefsAfter curing, the shells are used alongside concrete structures to create complex surfaces where oysters can settle. Oyster larvae need hard substrate to attach to as they develop, making old oyster shells particularly useful for reef restoration. The Billion Oyster Project seeds prepared reef material with oyster larvae before the structures are placed at restoration sites around New York Harbor. As the oysters grow, they form clusters that gradually create more complex reef habitat. The aim is not simply to place individual oysters in the water but to recreate functioning reef communities that can support other marine organisms. Over time, the restored structures can become living parts of the harbour rather than simply artificial objects on the seafloor.More than 200 million oysters have been restoredThe shell-recycling programme is one part of a much larger effort. The Billion Oyster Project currently says that more than 200 million oysters have been restored to New York Harbor. Its latest 2025 monitoring report recorded more than 180 million live oysters restored by the end of that year, showing how quickly the cumulative restoration figure has continued to grow. The organisation has also reported about 19 acres of restored reef habitat. These numbers represent years of work involving restaurants, scientists, educators, volunteers and harbour restoration teams. The project ultimately wants the restored oyster population to reach a scale at which reefs can become increasingly self-sustaining and reproduce naturally.New York Harbor once had enormous oyster reefsOyster restoration is particularly significant because oysters were once an important part of New York Harborâs ecosystem. Before large-scale urban development, pollution and intensive harvesting transformed the harbour, extensive oyster reefs covered large areas of its waters. Oysters were also a major part of New Yorkâs food economy, with the city's oyster industry once supporting enormous harvests. Over time, however, pollution, habitat destruction, overharvesting and changes to the harbour environment caused the oyster population to collapse. The Billion Oyster Project is attempting to reverse part of that historical loss by rebuilding reefs and reintroducing oysters to suitable areas of the harbour.Restored oysters can filter harbour waterOysters are more than just reef-building animals. They are filter feeders that remove suspended particles from the water as they feed. A large and healthy oyster population can therefore contribute to clearer water and improved conditions within an ecosystem. The benefits can extend beyond the oysters themselves because reefs provide shelter and surfaces for other marine organisms. The Billion Oyster Project's latest monitoring work recorded 44 different taxa of fish, crabs, shrimp and other invertebrates using restored reef areas. That suggests the developing reefs are functioning as habitat for a broader community of marine life rather than simply serving as places where transplanted oysters are kept.Oyster reefs can support coastal resilienceThe restored reefs may also contribute to New York's wider efforts to make its waterfront more resilient. Oyster reefs can absorb some wave energy and create natural habitat along coastal areas, making them an example of nature-based infrastructure. They are not a replacement for engineered flood protection, but healthy reef systems can form part of a broader strategy for protecting coastal ecosystems. Their value comes from combining several functions at once. The reefs provide habitat, support biodiversity, filter water and can help reduce the energy of waves reaching vulnerable shorelines. That makes oyster restoration relevant not only to conservation but also to the long-term environmental resilience of New York Harbor.The project has a much bigger goalThe Billion Oyster Project's name reflects its long-term ambition to restore one billion oysters to New York Harbor by 2030. The organisation also aims to involve one million students in its education programmes. Reaching that scale would represent a major increase from the harbour's current restored population and could help create conditions in which oyster reefs become more capable of sustaining themselves. The project is therefore measuring its progress through more than the number of shells collected from restaurants. It is also monitoring oyster survival, growth, reproduction and the wider communities of marine life that use restored reefs.Restaurant waste is becoming part of a living ecosystemThe most striking part of the programme is the transformation taking place between a restaurant kitchen and the harbour floor. A shell left behind after a meal might once have gone directly into the waste stream. Instead, it can now be collected, cured, placed into a reef structure and eventually become the surface on which a young oyster settles. As those oysters grow, they can create habitat used by fish, crabs, shrimp and other organisms. With more than 3.2 million pounds of shells collected so far and about 19 acres of reef habitat restored, New York City's restaurant waste is becoming an unlikely building material for bringing parts of its historic harbour ecosystem back to life.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ex-chief constable being investigated by IOPC over Israeli fan ban
articles.summary: Craig Guildford, three police officers and a staff member face IOPC investigation.
articles.body:
The former chief constable of West Midlands Police is being investigated by the police watchdog for gross misconduct over the banning of Israeli Maccabi Tel Aviv fans from a match against Aston Villa.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has given notice that it is investigating Craig Guildford, as well as three police officers and a staff member.

An independent investigation was launched by the IOPC in January to examine the involvement of West Midlands Police officers in the planning and preparation of the match at Villa Park on 6 November 2025.

The ban attracted national and international debate, with the government saying it would do everything in its power to overturn it.

Maccabi supporters were barred from travelling to the game following safety concerns based on an inaccurate report prepared by West Midlands Police.

Eight errors were found in the report, including overstating Maccabi supporters' role in disorder in Amsterdam in 2024, and a reference to a non-existent game between Maccabi and West Ham, said to have been produced by Microsoft Copilot.

The decision to impose the ban was made by Birmingham's Safety Advisory Group (SAG), which included representatives from bodies including West Midlands Police and Birmingham City Council.

The IOPC said evidence indicated that Guildford "may have had oversight on an intelligence briefing document presented to the safety advisory group (SAG) that was later reported to have contained inaccuracies and misleading information".

It is alleged the briefing document "gave an imbalanced view of the risk away fans posed", contributing to the decision to ban the supporters.

The police watchdog added: "We consider Mr Guildford may have failed to ensure due diligence and the highest level of scrutiny over such an influential document."

Guildford retired from the force after both Downing Street and the home secretary said they had lost confidence in his leadership .

Announcing his retirement, Guildford did not offer an apology and blamed what he described as the "political and media frenzy" for his decision to step down.

A senior serving officer, who played a lead role in compiling the briefing, is under investigation for allegedly failing to ensure its accuracy.

The watchdog said the officer may not have accurately represented some information which could have resulted in the briefing "lacking impartiality".

They are also examining whether the officer "may have failed to appropriately handle sensitive intelligence" contained in the report, before it was shared with SAG members.

The staff member, who was involved in researching and compiling intelligence for the game, is alleged to have sourced inaccurate information from AI searches and took no subsequent action to help ensure it was not included in briefings.

Two other senior serving officers who played important roles in the force's planning for the game have been notified they are being investigated for potential misconduct.

It is alleged one was not sufficiently diligent in the exercise of their duties in overseeing the operation, including balancing operational needs alongside engaging with local Jewish communities, and that they displayed a lack of impartiality towards Maccabi fans in both external and internal communications.

The other officer will be investigated in relation to their oversight of the briefing document and an allegation that they too lacked balance in references to Maccabi supporters.

A dedicated investigation team at the IOPC has examined more than 600 pieces of evidence, including operational documents, reports, intelligence research, minutes of meetings, and a large volume of correspondence including emails and messages.

The IOPC's director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, said: "Our investigation to date has been to assess whether there is an indication anyone may have breached one or more of the standards of police professional behaviour.

"We have examined a wealth of material, hundreds of pieces of evidence, and believe there is an indication some people serving with the police may potentially have behaved in a manner that could justify disciplinary proceedings.

"They have been informed their conduct will be investigated. At the end of our investigation, we will decide if anyone has a case to answer and should face a misconduct meeting or hearing."

Campbell added that the serving of notices did not necessarily mean that disciplinary proceedings would follow, saying all decisions would be kept under review as the investigation progressed.

West Midlands Police's temporary deputy chief constable, Jen Mattinson, said that she undertook a voluntary referral to the IOPC on her first full day in the role regarding conduct matters by senior officers and staff.

"This referral was made prior to the IOPC announcement to use their 'power of initiative' to independently investigate if any officer or staff member may have a case to answer for misconduct," Mattinson said.

"We recognise that the public's trust in West Midlands Police has been damaged by this event and we have worked hard over the last seven months - and continue to do so - to rebuild confidence in the force.

"We will continue to fully engage and cooperate with the IOPC as their work continues."

West Midlands Police admitted that it "overstated the evidence" used to make the decision to ban the Maccabi Tel Aviv fans, in documents released in January .

The force said "we did not engage early enough with the local Jewish community", and indicated there was now a ban on AI use after its evidence included a match that did not take place.

Furthermore, it said its operations would have lasted four days, involved multiple forces, and cost more than £5m, if 2,500 away fans had attended.

articles.title: In 1962, IBM built a secret NSA computer that ran jobs up to 200 times faster than any other machine; 14 years later a worn-out part ended its run because its maker was no longer in business
articles.summary: Tech News News: IBM built a secret computer for the US National Security Agency that began operating in 1962 and remained in service for 14 years, processing some of .
articles.body: IBM built a secret computer for the US National Security Agency that began operating in 1962 and remained in service for 14 years, processing some of the agency's most sensitive cryptographic workloads during the Cold War. Known as Harvest, the machine could run certain jobs up to 200 times faster than other computers of its time, according to accounts of its capabilities.According to a report by IEEE Spectrum, Harvest finally stopped running on February 27, 1976, after a mechanical component in its automated tape library wore out. The manufacturer of the part was no longer in business, leaving the NSA without a practical way to replace it. By then, the machine had operated through the Cuban Missile Crisis, the Vietnam War, and the period leading up to the 1975 Helsinki Accords.IBM built Harvest as a specialised NSA computerHarvest was officially designated the IBM 7950 and was built around IBM's 7030 Stretch mainframe. IBM developed Stretch for scientific computing, but the NSA needed a system that could continuously process large volumes of intercepted communications without requiring operators to manually stage each batch of tape.After two unsuccessful proposals, IBM secured the NSA contract in 1958. The resulting system combined Stretch with a custom streaming processor and an automated tape-storage system called Tractor.Unlike a general-purpose computer, Harvest's custom processor was designed to repeatedly apply a fixed sequence of operations to data streams. It could take two streams, known as P and Q, from memory, process them and return the result as a third stream, R.The processor used overlapping stages, or a pipeline, so that while one pair of data bytes was being processed, the next could already be fetched from memory. Harvest shared memory with Stretch and could address individual bits rather than being restricted to complete bytes or words.Its processing units included a logic unit for bitwise operations and a table-lookup unit that could use incoming data to address information in memory.Harvest processed large volumes of intercepted dataThe NSA used Harvest for cryptanalytic and large-scale text-processing jobs. One documented example described the machine searching 3.5 billion characters of text for any of 7,000 target terms in just under four hours.Another job, referred to as âMoretown,â involved searching 11 million messages covering 16 years of intercepted traffic against about 8,000 search terms. NSA analyst Robert Looney said in 1972 that the job took about 10 hours, although he did not disclose the purpose of the search.As a complete system, Harvest could stream one byte every 0.3 microseconds and had about 800 kilobytes of addressable memory.IBM engineer Frances Allen, who worked on both Stretch and Harvest, later recalled the type of operations the machine could perform.âIt was quite an amazing computer,â Allen said in a 2001 oral history. âOne instruction, for example, could do sorts, and do statistical analysis of the data that was streaming by it.â¦ Everything we were doing at that time was on the cutting edge. There was no question about it.âHarvest's specialised design also created challenges within the NSA. According to James Bamford's 2001 history of the agency, some officials reportedly looked at the machine during employee tours and said, âItâs beautiful, but it doesnât work.âThe system nonetheless continued to handle large jobs that general-purpose machines were not well suited to process.IBM built Tractor to keep Harvest supplied with dataHarvest's processing capacity required a storage system that could supply large datasets without constant human intervention. IBM therefore built Tractor, an automated magnetic-tape library officially designated the IBM 7955.Each Tractor cassette weighed about 6 to 7 kilograms and contained roughly 120 megabytes of data on a 550-metre reel of tape. Each storage unit could hold up to 160 cassettes.When Harvest began operating in 1962, three automatic cartridge units were connected to it, each serving two tape drives. Together, they provided about 44 gigabytes of online storage.The automated system used a motor-driven arm to retrieve cassettes from storage racks and deliver them to tape drives. The mechanism could move at about 6 metres per second, while software running on Stretch controlled cassette movement and data reading and writing.Moving from one completed tape to the next could take about 18 seconds, once the next cassette had been retrieved and was ready to mount. Retrieving and preparing a cassette did not require manual handling.Tractor therefore functioned as both long-term storage and a source of data for Harvest's processing jobs. Conventional reel-to-reel drives connected to Stretch were also used when large datasets had to be transferred into or out of the system.Harvest had its own programming languageIBM and the NSA also developed a programming language specifically for Harvest. Called Alpha, short for Advanced Language for Programming Harvest, it was designed around the machine's streaming architecture and the needs of cryptanalysts.Alpha allowed programmers to define the alphabet used for cryptographic data and included symbols for representing uncertain or null characters. A âscab,â represented by a question mark, indicated a character that was known to exist but whose identity was unknown. A blank space represented a âpad,â or null character.The language also provided ways to combine strings into larger structures, giving programmers a way to describe complex intercepted messages and cryptanalytic datasets.Allen worked on the Harvest software and later recalled that the technical report she produced for her part of the project disappeared into the NSA's classified system after she completed it.âI spent the good part of a summer on that,â she recalled in 2001. âAnd it just disappeared into Fort Meade somewhere.âHarvest's secrecy also shaped how some IBM employees understood the project. Allen said the NSA was not widely known outside classified intelligence circles when she began working on the machine, so she initially believed she was working on a naval project. The budget code name for the NSA was âBureau of Ships.âHarvest remained in use as newer computers arrivedBy 1971, Harvest was operating about 115 hours a week, according to Looney, representing more than two-thirds of its available operating time. At the same time, the number of jobs it handled had been declining since 1967 as newer general-purpose computers took over ordinary data-processing work.Harvest was increasingly reserved for large, specialised workloads that other machines could not handle as efficiently.At the system's 10th anniversary in 1972, Looney described it as a machine âconceived in the fifties, born in the sixties, and irreplaceable in the seventies.âThe description did not last much longer.On February 27, 1976, operators shut Harvest down for the final time. A mechanical component in the Tractor tape library had worn out, and the company that manufactured the part was no longer operating. Replacing the system's ageing hardware was no longer practical.The NSA marked the occasion with a mock telegram written in Harvest's name. âI first began operations at NSA. Although not widely known, I was probably the largest, fastest, and most technically advanced computer system in the world,â it said. âAnd now, fourteen years later, the time to retire has come. The cost of my upkeep and operation has been overtaken by more modern equipment and the newer technologies.âThe NSA replaced Harvest with the Cray-1The NSA eventually replaced Harvest with the Cray-1 supercomputer. Unlike Harvest, the Cray-1 used newer integrated circuits and was designed primarily for numerical and scientific computing, but its processing capabilities also made it suitable for workloads that had previously required Harvest's specialised hardware.The Cray-1 was also commercially available to multiple customers, unlike Harvest, which had been built specifically for the NSA. As newer general-purpose and scientific systems improved, maintaining a custom machine for one specialised workload became less practical.Harvest did not have a direct line of successors, partly because its architecture was built around the NSA's particular requirements. Several of its concepts, however, appeared later in other areas of computing.Tractor's automated tape library anticipated robotic storage systems later used in large data centres. Harvest's pipeline architecture also resembled approaches that became part of dataflow computing, while its continuous pattern-matching operations have parallels in later systems designed to inspect network traffic.Harvest's operational life ended with a worn mechanical part and an unavailable manufacturer, but the ideas used to build the system continued to appear in computing systems developed after it.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: This prehistoric Czech sanctuary is 1,000 years older than Stonehenge; reveals how farmers tracked the movements of the Sun and the Moon 6,500 years ago
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A prehistoric sanctuary discovered near Chleby in the Czech Republic is giving archaeologists a brand new view of how Europeâs early farming communiti.
articles.body: A prehistoric sanctuary discovered near Chleby in the Czech Republic is giving archaeologists a brand new view of how Europe’s early farming communities understood the Sun, Moon and changing seasons. The circular structure, built more than 6,500 years ago, is around 1,000 years older than Stonehenge and appears to have been designed for both rituals and observing movements in the sky. According to the University of West Bohemia (UWB), archaeologists have found that the enormous enclosure contained 12 entrances whose positions were carefully arranged rather than placed randomly. Their research suggests that people who lived in the region had a detailed understanding of important solar and lunar cycles. The discovery makes the Chleby sanctuary one of the oldest monuments of its kind in Central Europe and offers a rare glimpse into prehistoric beliefs and daily life.What makes the 6,500-year-old Czech sanctuary so uniqueThe sanctuary stands near the present-day village of Chleby and dates back more than 6,500 years. As per the University of West Bohemia's report, people constructed an almost circular enclosure measuring about 230 metres across. The structure was surrounded by a ditch more than 2.5 metres deep and contained 12 entrances. What initially appeared to be a prehistoric enclosure became even more significant when archaeologists examined the positioning of those entrances. Petr Krištuf from the Department of Archaeology at the University of West Bohemia, leads the research and explained that circular enclosures from this period are completely unknown in the region. The arrangement of the entrances therefore provided an important clue that the site had been deliberately designed. Instead of simply forming a large enclosed area, the structure appears to have been created around particular points on the horizon.Prehistoric Chleby farmers tracking the Sun and the MoonThe positioning of the entrances appears to have allowed people at Chleby to observe important events in movements of the Sun and the Moon. The research team has identified two main observation points. One is connected with the Moon's extreme positions on the horizon during its approximately 18-year cycle. The other links sunrise at the summer solstice with sunset at the winter solstice. According to the University of West Bohemia, this arrangement is similar to the better-known alignment at Stonehenge. The major difference is its age. Organic material recovered from Chleby indicates that the sanctuary was established more than 1,000 years before Stonehenge. For the farming communities who built it, these celestial events may have carried meanings beyond simply marking dates. Krištuf said that sunrise at the summer solstice could have represented a beginning, while sunset at the winter solstice represented an ending. The layout of the sanctuary suggests that these ideas may have been built directly into the landscape.Ritualistic belief connected with the Chleby sanctuaryThe evidence suggests that the sanctuary was not simply an early astronomical observation site. Archaeologists have also discovered remains that point towards ritual activities. Bull skulls and horns were found in the ditch close to the entrances. Archaeologists believe that these remains may once have decorated large gateways leading into the enclosure. Jan Turek, an archaeologist involved in the research on behalf of Charles University, noted that the bull was an important religious symbol among Europe's first farming communities and was known from several parts of prehistoric Europe. The combination of carefully positioned entrances and animal remains therefore gives the site a more complex character. The sanctuary has connected observations of the natural world with ceremonies and beliefs. Human remains add another layer to the story. Earlier research identified a Bronze Age burial belonging to the Únětice culture. Around 18 people were buried there gradually over time.Did the sanctuary remain important for thousands of yearsAccording to the University of West Bohemia, current research suggests that its role eventually changed. By the Iron Age, the monument appears to have lost its original significance. The ditch was gradually filled in, and an ordinary settlement was established where the former sanctuary had stood. This development contrasts with the history of Stonehenge, which experienced repeated periods of renewed use and continued to acquire cultural associations long after its construction. At Chleby, the evidence points towards a gradual fading of the monument's original importance. What had once been a significant ritual landscape eventually became part of everyday settlement.Learnings from the prehistoric Czech siteThe research at Chleby is now turning particular attention to the soil surrounding and within the enclosure. Jan Fišer of the University of Hradec Králové is analysing soil samples because human activity can leave chemical traces even when visible objects have disappeared. According to the university, these traces could help researchers understand how the site was used during different periods of prehistory. That could reveal details that artefacts alone cannot provide. It may help establish where particular activities took place and how the use of the sanctuary changed over time. The Chleby discovery ultimately shows that sophisticated prehistoric monuments were not limited to famous sites such as Stonehenge. More than 6,500 years ago, farming communities in what is now the Czech Republic were already creating large structures whose design appears to have connected the land, the seasons and the movements of celestial bodies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A New Zealand sailor spent years living alone on a remote Cook Islands atoll across three separate stays; a year after his final stay ended, Suwarrow was declared a national park
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A remote Pacific atoll that was once the solitary kingdom of a New Zealand sailor has secured a lasting future, transforming from a hermit's retreat i.
articles.body: A remote Pacific atoll that was once the solitary kingdom of a New Zealand sailor has secured a lasting future, transforming from a hermit's retreat into the first conservation sanctuary in the Cook Islands. Suwarrow, an isolated coral atoll about 1,300 kilometres north of Rarotonga, was officially declared a national park in 1978. The decision came just one year after its most famous resident, Tom Neale, ended his final stay on the island. Neale spent about 16 years living as a solitary beachcomber on Anchorage Island, the main islet in the Suwarrow atoll. His life there, described in his 1966 autobiography An Island to Oneself, turned the tiny island into a symbol of complete isolation. Today, government records and historical archives document how the remote retreat became an important environmental reserve.A life of deliberate isolationBorn in Wellington, New Zealand, in 1902, Neale joined the Royal New Zealand Navy as a young man before buying out his contract to travel independently around the Pacific. He later worked on several islands as a trader and storekeeper. He eventually met American author Robert Dean Frisbie, whose stories about Suwarrow inspired Neale to seek a quiet life on the remote atoll. Neale first visited Suwarrow in 1945 while delivering supplies to wartime coast-watchers. He was fascinated by the small ring of coral and spent years getting permission and gathering supplies to live there. In October 1952, Neale arrived on the uninhabited atoll with two cats, a radio, tools and basic supplies. He lived there during three separate periods: from 1952 to 1954, 1960 to 1963, and 1967 to 1977. During his stays, he repaired abandoned huts, grew vegetables, raised chickens and relied mainly on fish, breadfruit and coconut crabs for food.Explaining why he chose to leave modern society behind, Neale wrote in his autobiography: "I chose to live in the Pacific islands because life there moves at the sort of pace which you feel God must have had in mind originally when He made the sun to keep us warm and provided the fruits of the earth for the taking." His isolated life was eventually brought to an end by health problems. He suffered a serious back injury during his first stay and was diagnosed with stomach cancer during his final period on the island. He left Suwarrow for good in March 1977 and died in Rarotonga later that year at the age of 75.From remote retreat to national parkAfter Neale's departure and death, the Cook Islands government moved to protect the natural environment of the atoll he had called home. In 1978, the entire atoll, its surrounding reef and a six-kilometre marine area were declared the country's first national park and bird sanctuary. Official environmental records maintained by the National Library of New Zealand and the Cook Islands National Environment Service describe Suwarrow as an important ecological sanctuary. Protecting the atoll as a park helped shield its fragile habitats from commercial development and uncontrolled exploitation. The Cook Islands National Environment Service also maintains strict rules for the area. Visitors need permission to enter, while vessels must obtain permits before arriving.A haven for wildlifeAlthough Neale made Suwarrow famous among sailors and readers around the world, the atoll's greatest value lies in its wildlife. The reef system includes 30 small islets, or motus, surrounding a sheltered central lagoon. Together, they form one of the important seabird breeding areas in the South Pacific. Regional environmental surveys show that Suwarrow supports roughly nine per cent of the world's Lesser Frigatebird population. It also has important breeding colonies of Red-tailed Tropicbirds and Sooty Terns. The surrounding waters support coconut crabs, green sea turtles and several shark species. To protect these animals, the national park is left without permanent human habitation for part of the year. From November to March, during the Pacific cyclone season, people are not allowed to stay on the atoll, giving wildlife a period with little human disturbance.Neale's legacy on Anchorage IslandMore than four decades after Neale's final departure, signs of his life remain on Anchorage Island. The small wooden hut he repaired and lived in has been preserved by seasonal park caretakers. Part of it has been turned into a small lending library for sailors and passing yachtsmen. A concrete bust of the New Zealand sailor also stands nearby as a tribute to his remarkable life. Today, two caretakers stay on the island during the dry season. They manage visitors, monitor bird populations and help protect the fragile environment. Neale came to Suwarrow in search of solitude and a simple life. His story, however, helped bring international attention to the remote atoll and its natural beauty. What began as one man's private escape from modern society eventually became a protected sanctuary designed to keep the island's wildlife and wilderness intact for generations. A closer look at Tom Neale's extraordinary life on Suwarrow can be found in the archival documentary Tom Neale: Man Who Lived Alone on a Remote Island. The footage provides historical context on Neale's daily life, his survival on Anchorage Island and the years he spent living alone in one of the Pacific's most isolated corners.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
